topic: morph-aware-reps — Morphology-aware representation learning for morphologically rich / agglutinative languages, with emphasis on Turkish and on what transfers to a morphology-aware dual-encoder retrieval system

papers.title: Morpheus: A Morphology-Aware Neural Tokenizer and Word Embedder for Turkish
papers.approach: Joint neural tokenizer + word embedder. Per-character morpheme-boundary probabilities are turned into soft segment assignments during training via a differentiable Poisson-binomial dynamic program, and hard segments at inference; the abstract states lossless round-trip tokenization (decode(encode(w)) = w) holds by construction. Morphology is injected by learning morpheme boundaries rather than corpus-statistical merges, so suffix-bearing units are not fragmented.
papers.key_results: Abstract page reports: bits-per-character 1.425 (lowest among the reversible tokenizers compared); MorphScore macro-F1 0.61 vs ~0.32 for subword tokenizers; ~19% less GPU memory than 64K-vocab subword models; root-family lexical retrieval MAP 0.85 and same-root verification ROC-AUC 1.00, reported as beating BGE-M3 and BERTurk on those lexical tasks. The paper concedes contextual encoders stay ahead on NER and case/number probing, attributed to Morpheus's root-centric geometry.
papers.why_relevant: Closest existing artifact to your 'morphological channel encoder': a lightweight Turkish-specific encoder whose embedding space is explicitly organised by root/suffix structure, and which is explicitly weaker on context-dependent semantics — exactly the complementarity a two-channel design assumes. Its root-family MAP / same-root ROC-AUC tasks are also a ready-made probe design.

papers.title: Impact of Tokenization on Language Models: An Analysis for Turkish
papers.approach: Pretrains and fine-tunes Turkish LMs under five tokenizers spanning granularities (character, word, morphological-level, WordPiece, BPE) and compares on six downstream tasks, sweeping vocabulary size.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports the morphological-level tokenizer gives competitive but not superior performance vs de facto WordPiece/BPE; increasing vocabulary size benefits morphological- and word-level tokenizers more than WordPiece/BPE; suggests ~20% vocabulary-to-parameter ratio for WordPiece/BPE vs ~40% for the others.
papers.why_relevant: The main cautionary data point: for Turkish, swapping in morpheme segmentation alone did not beat BPE/WordPiece on downstream tasks. Argues for adding a morphology channel alongside a strong subword semantic encoder rather than replacing its tokenizer.

papers.title: Optimal Turkish Subword Strategies at Scale: Systematic Evaluation of Data–Vocabulary–Morphology Interplay
papers.approach: Jointly varies tokenizer vocabulary size and tokenizer-training corpus size under matched parameter budgets across WordPiece, morphology-level and character baselines; evaluates on semantic (NLI, STS, sentiment, NER), syntactic (POS, dependency parsing) and morphology-sensitive probes. Introduces a morphology-aware diagnostic toolkit: boundary micro/macro-F1 against gold morpheme boundaries, lemma atomicity vs surface boundary hits, over-/under-segmentation indices, CER/WER, continuation rate, affix-type coverage.
papers.key_results: I did not read the results tables — only the abstract/summary describing the framework and the claim that it identifies when character-level and morphology-level tokenization pay off.
papers.why_relevant: Its intrinsic diagnostics (boundary F1, over/under-segmentation, affix coverage) are directly reusable as cheap, gold-annotation-based metrics to characterise the tokenizers of your candidate semantic encoders before any fine-tuning, and to justify model-selection choices.

papers.title: Tokens with Meaning: A Hybrid Tokenization Approach for Turkish
papers.authors_short: Bayram, Fincan, Gümüş, Karakaş, Diri, Yıldırım, Çelik
papers.approach: Three-stage hybrid: dictionary-driven root/affix segmentation, phonological normalization that maps allomorphs (vowel-harmony/consonant-alternation variants) to a single canonical affix identifier, and a controlled subword fallback for OOV. Released vocabulary: 22,231 roots mapped to 20,000 canonical ids, 72 affix ids covering 177 allomorphic surface forms, 12,696 subword units, one casing token.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports 90.29% Turkish Token Percentage and 85.80% Pure Token Percentage; claims gains over CosmosGPT2, Mursit and Tabi baselines on Turkish STS Benchmark and MTEB-TR, and strongest average accuracy on TurBLiMP. I did not verify per-task numbers.
papers.why_relevant: The allomorph-canonicalization idea is the single most transferable trick for a Turkish morphology channel: -ler/-lar, -di/-dı/-du/-dü etc. collapse to one symbol, so the morph encoder sees the *feature* rather than the surface string. Also a plausible source of typed negatives for your synthetic eval set (swap one canonical affix id, keep the root).

papers.title: HeceTokenizer: A Syllable-Based Tokenization Approach for Turkish Retrieval
papers.approach: Phonology- rather than morphology-driven: exploits Turkish's six deterministic syllable patterns to build a closed, OOV-free vocabulary of roughly 8,000 syllable types. Encoder is a BERT-tiny (~1.5M params) trained from scratch on Turkish Wikipedia with MLM, then used for retrieval.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports 50.3% Recall@5 on TQuAD retrieval for the syllable tokenizer, versus 46.92% Recall@5 for a morphology-driven baseline that the abstract describes as a ~200x larger model. BPE/WordPiece baselines are not stated in the abstract.
papers.why_relevant: Direct evidence that a tiny, linguistically-structured Turkish encoder can be retrieval-useful at ~1.5M parameters — a realistic size envelope for your morphological channel encoder. Also a warning that syllable structure, not just morpheme structure, may be carrying part of the signal you attribute to morphology.

papers.title: TurkColBERT: A Benchmark of Dense and Late-Interaction Models for Turkish Information Retrieval
papers.approach: Benchmarks 10 dense and late-interaction (ColBERT-style) models on five Turkish BEIR datasets. Not morphology-injection per se; the relevant mechanism is token-level MaxSim interaction instead of a single pooled vector.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports ColmmBERT-base-TR up to +13.8% mAP on domain-specific tasks, and colbert-hash-nano-tr (1.0M params) retaining over 71% of the average mAP of turkish-e5-large (600M). Headline claim: late-interaction models 3-5x smaller significantly outperform dense encoders. The abstract does not itself analyse morphology or tokenization.
papers.why_relevant: Strong baseline context for your project and an architectural alternative you should be able to argue against: late interaction already recovers much of the sub-word/lexical matching a morphology channel is meant to supply. Any two-channel result should be compared to a ColBERT-style Turkish baseline, not only to a single-vector dense one.

papers.title: Adapting Multilingual Embedding Models to Turkish via Cross-Lingual Tokenizer Surgery and Offline Distillation
papers.approach: 'Tokenizer surgery': builds a Turkish-optimized multilingual vocabulary (131,072) by pruning redundant teacher tokens and re-adding multilingual tokens by frequency over a 40-language corpus; re-initializes the embedding table by mean-composition token mapping while keeping the transformer backbone; then offline embedding distillation from precomputed teacher vectors with a cosine objective on balanced 40-language Wikipedia.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports STSb-TR Pearson/Spearman 77.55/77.45 for the ~200M student vs 73.84/72.92 for the ~300M teacher, and TR-MTEB mean 63.9% (7th of 26 models), 8,192-token context. No explicit morphology analysis in the abstract.
papers.why_relevant: A concrete, cheap recipe for making a multilingual semantic encoder tokenize Turkish sensibly without retraining, and evidence that fixing fragmentation alone already moves Turkish STS/MTEB. Useful as a pre-step or as an ablation arm ('better Turkish tokenization' vs 'explicit morphology channel').

papers.title: Hierarchical Multi Task Learning with Subword Contextual Embeddings for Languages with Rich Morphology
papers.approach: Hierarchical multi-task learning over dependency parsing and NER, using subword contextual embeddings to carry morphological information instead of an external morphological analyzer / manual annotation. Five multi-task configurations compared.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports 18.86% F1 improvement on dependency parsing and 4.61% F1 on NER over a previous multi-task learner for Turkish, and claims SOTA on both at the time. Note: the abstract does not describe a separate morphological-tagging auxiliary head — morphology enters implicitly via subword contextual embeddings.
papers.why_relevant: Evidence that for Turkish, subword contextual embeddings plus task hierarchy can substitute for an explicit morphological analyzer. Tempers the assumption that you need a hand-built morph channel; also a template if you add a morphological-tagging auxiliary loss to the LoRA fine-tune.

papers.title: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information
papers.language_focus: Multilingual (9 languages, incl. morphologically rich ones)
papers.approach: Skip-gram where each word is a bag of character n-grams; the word vector is the sum of its n-gram vectors, giving compositional, OOV-capable representations. The canonical fastText subword model.
papers.key_results: Paper reports state-of-the-art word similarity/analogy results across nine languages versus prior morphological word-representation methods; I did not read the per-language tables.
papers.why_relevant: The cheapest possible morphological channel: a character-n-gram bag encoder is trivially trainable on Turkish, has no OOV, and naturally puts inflected forms of one root near each other. A strong, honest baseline your neural morph encoder must beat.

papers.title: Better Word Representations with Recursive Neural Networks for Morphology
papers.approach: Recursive neural network over a morphemic decomposition (morpheme = basic unit), combined with a neural language model, so rare/complex words are composed from their morphemes rather than assigned independent vectors.
papers.key_results: Reported improvements on rare/complex word representation; I did not read the result tables.
papers.why_relevant: The original 'compose the word vector from its morphemes' architecture. For Turkish, root + ordered suffix sequence composition is the direct analogue, and a recursive/sequential composer over Zemberek-style analyses is a viable morph-channel design.

papers.title: Character-Aware Neural Language Models
papers.language_focus: Multilingual: Arabic, Czech, French, German, Spanish, Russian, English
papers.approach: Character-level CNN plus a highway network feeding a word-level LSTM LM — no word embeddings, no morphological supervision; morphology emerges from character convolutions.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports parity with SOTA on English PTB with 60% fewer parameters, and outperforming word-level and morpheme-level LSTM baselines on the morphologically rich languages, again with fewer parameters.
papers.why_relevant: The char-CNN+highway block is a small, fast, drop-in encoder for the morphological channel and needs no analyzer. Notably it beat *morpheme-level* baselines, which is an argument for character-level rather than analyzer-based morph channels.

papers.title: Morphological Word-Embeddings
papers.approach: Semi-supervised: extends the log-bilinear model with a term that uses morphologically annotated data, so words sharing morphological features are pulled together in the embedding space.
papers.key_results: Paper demonstrates the learned embeddings place morphologically similar words nearby; I did not read numeric tables.
papers.why_relevant: The cleanest precedent for supervising an embedding space with morphological tags — the same idea as adding a morphological-tag-prediction auxiliary loss or a morph-feature contrastive term on top of your LoRA fine-tune.

papers.title: Superbizarre Is Not Superb: Derivational Morphology Improves BERT's Interpretation of Complex Words
papers.approach: DelBERT: feeds BERT a derivational (morpheme-respecting) input segmentation instead of WordPiece, and probes semantic representations of complex/novel words. Frames PLMs as serial dual-route models where complex-word meaning is either stored or composed from subwords.
papers.key_results: Abstract claims DelBERT substantially outperforms WordPiece-segmented BERT on the semantic probing tasks; I did not read the exact scores.
papers.why_relevant: Best-argued evidence that segmentation quality changes *semantic* generalization, not just perplexity — and its dual-route framing is essentially the conceptual justification for a two-channel (stored-lexical vs composed-morphological) encoder.

papers.title: MorphTE: Injecting Morphology in Tensorized Embeddings
papers.approach: Represents a word embedding as a tensor-product entanglement of its morpheme vectors, so morpheme vectors are shared across words; morpheme count and dimension are far smaller than the word vocabulary.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports ~20x compression of word-embedding parameters without performance loss on MT and QA, and gains over other embedding-compression methods. I did not read the tables.
papers.why_relevant: A concrete parameter-efficient way to build a morphology channel whose *entire* embedding table is morpheme-indexed — attractive when the morph encoder must be lightweight next to a full semantic encoder.

papers.title: MorphBPE: A Morpho-Aware Tokenizer Bridging Linguistic Complexity for Efficient LLM Training Across Morphologies
papers.approach: Constrains BPE merges to respect morpheme boundaries — keeps BPE's statistical efficiency while adding linguistic structure. Introduces two evaluation metrics: Morphological Consistency F1 and Morphological Edit Distance.
papers.key_results: Abstract claims consistently reduced cross-entropy loss, faster convergence and improved morphological alignment at 300M and 1B scales across the four languages. No downstream retrieval numbers.
papers.why_relevant: Hungarian is agglutinative and behaves similarly to Turkish, so this is the closest cross-language replication. Its two alignment metrics are directly usable to score your candidate encoders' tokenizers on Turkish gold segmentations.

papers.title: MorphPiece: A Linguistic Tokenizer for Large Language Models
papers.approach: Tokenization partly based on morphological segmentation; a GPT-style model (MorphGPT) is trained on it and compared against GPT-2 with standard BPE.
papers.key_results: Search summary reports superior convergence and language-modeling performance described as comparable to a ~6x larger BPE model, plus better supervised and unsupervised downstream results vs GPT-2. I did not read the paper itself; treat these numbers as unverified.
papers.why_relevant: Frequently cited as the strong-positive counterexample to the Turkish tokenization results — useful to cite for balance, with the caveat that it is English-only and the comparison protocol has been contested.

papers.title: Improving Korean NLP Tasks with Linguistically Informed Subword Tokenization and Sub-character Decomposition
papers.approach: Morpheme-aware pipeline: pre-tokenize with a morphological analyzer, then apply BPE/WordPiece; plus Hangul sub-character (jamo) decomposition. A key engineering point noted in search results is using only the BPE model at inference so no analyzer is needed at serving time.
papers.key_results: Search summary reports morpheme-analysis + BPE beating BPE-only and sub-character-only tokenization, and morpheme-based WordPiece beating character-based Korean BERTs (HanBERT, KorBERT). I did not read the tables.
papers.why_relevant: The 'analyzer at training time, analyzer-free at inference' trick solves the main deployment objection to a Zemberek-dependent morphological channel in a retrieval system that must encode queries at low latency.

papers.title: Morphosyntactic probing of multilingual BERT models
papers.approach: Trains probing classifiers to recover morphological tags from mBERT-family representations, layer by layer, across many languages.
papers.key_results: I only saw summary-level claims (morphological information is recoverable, varies by layer and language); no numbers verified. Year and author list not confirmed.
papers.why_relevant: Methodological template for your morph-sensitivity probe: it tells you whether the *existing* semantic encoder already encodes the suffix features, which determines whether a separate morph channel is adding signal or duplicating it. Run this before committing to the two-channel design.

techniques.name: Allomorph canonicalization of suffixes
techniques.description: Normalize vowel-harmony / consonant-alternation variants of the same Turkish morpheme to a single canonical identifier before encoding (e.g. -ler/-lar, -di/-dı/-du/-dü/-ti/-tı → one id). 'Tokens with Meaning' ships exactly this: 72 affix identifiers covering 177 surface allomorphs.
techniques.applicability: Highest-value, lowest-cost intervention for your morphological channel encoder. Feed the morph encoder a canonicalized [ROOT][AFFIX_ID_1][AFFIX_ID_2]... string so it learns the morphological *feature* rather than 177 orthographic strings. Also gives you a principled generator for morph_counterfactual negatives: swap one canonical affix id, hold the root fixed.
techniques.evidence: Bayram et al., 'Tokens with Meaning' (arXiv 2508.14292): reported vocabulary of 72 affix ids over 177 allomorphic forms, 90.29% Turkish Token Percentage, claimed gains on Turkish STS Benchmark and MTEB-TR.

techniques.name: Character-CNN + highway morph channel (analyzer-free)
techniques.description: A character-level convolution + highway stack as the morphological encoder. No morphological analyzer, no OOV, trivially fast, and it demonstrably picks up affixal structure.
techniques.applicability: The most deployable morph channel for a latency-sensitive dual encoder: a few million parameters, encodes queries in microseconds, sits next to a frozen/LoRA'd semantic encoder. Kim et al. found it beat morpheme-level LSTM baselines on morphologically rich languages, so it is a serious contender rather than just a baseline.
techniques.evidence: Kim, Jernite, Sontag & Rush, AAAI 2016 (arXiv 1508.06615): outperforms word-level and morpheme-level LSTM baselines on Arabic/Czech/French/German/Spanish/Russian with fewer parameters.

techniques.name: Character-n-gram bag (fastText-style) morph channel
techniques.description: Represent a word as the sum of its character n-gram vectors. Compositional, OOV-free, and inherently clusters inflected forms of one root.
techniques.applicability: Your mandatory cheap baseline. If a fastText-style morph channel gets most of the gain on your 50-query morph eval set, the neural morph encoder needs to justify itself. Train on Turkish Wikipedia + your corpus in under an hour.
techniques.evidence: Bojanowski, Grave, Joulin & Mikolov, TACL 2017: SOTA on word similarity/analogy across nine languages vs prior morphological word-representation methods.

techniques.name: Morpheme-boundary supervision with a differentiable segmenter
techniques.description: Train per-character boundary probabilities end-to-end (soft segments during training via dynamic programming, hard segments at inference), supervised or regularized toward gold morpheme boundaries, and pool the resulting segments into a word/passage embedding.
techniques.applicability: This is essentially the Morpheus recipe and the most direct blueprint for your morph channel. Its reported root-centric geometry — very strong same-root/root-family retrieval, weaker context-dependent semantics — is precisely the complement profile a two-channel system wants.
techniques.evidence: Şakar, 'Morpheus' (arXiv 2606.18717): MorphScore macro-F1 0.61 vs ~0.32 subword; root-family MAP 0.85; same-root ROC-AUC 1.00; reported above BGE-M3 and BERTurk on those lexical tasks, below contextual encoders on NER and case/number probing.

techniques.name: Morphology-constrained BPE (merge rules that respect morpheme boundaries)
techniques.description: Keep BPE's frequency-driven merges but forbid merges that cross a morpheme boundary, retaining compression while improving morphological alignment. Comes with two alignment metrics: Morphological Consistency F1 and Morphological Edit Distance.
techniques.applicability: If you ever retrain or extend the vocabulary of the morph channel, this is the segmentation policy to use. Even without retraining, the two alignment metrics are runnable today on your candidate semantic encoders' tokenizers against gold Turkish segmentations — a cheap, defensible extra column in your model-selection matrix.
techniques.evidence: Asgari, El Kheir & Sadraei Javaheri, MorphBPE (arXiv 2502.00894): reduced cross-entropy, faster convergence, improved morphological alignment across English/Russian/Hungarian/Arabic at 300M and 1B scale.

techniques.name: Analyzer at training time, analyzer-free at inference
techniques.description: Pre-tokenize training text with a morphological analyzer, learn a BPE/WordPiece model over the analyzer output, then at inference use only the learned subword model — the analyzer is never called in production.
techniques.applicability: Removes the main operational objection to a Zemberek-dependent morphological channel in a retrieval system where query encoding must be fast and dependency-light. Adopt this pattern if you build an analyzer-supervised morph channel.
techniques.evidence: Reported in the Korean morpheme-aware tokenization literature (arXiv 2311.03928 and related Korean tokenizer work); described in search summaries as improving both usability and speed while retaining the morpheme-aware gains.

techniques.name: Morphological-tag auxiliary loss / tag-guided embedding objective
techniques.description: Add a supervised term that pulls together forms sharing morphological features (or predicts morphological tags from the pooled representation) alongside the main objective, so the embedding space is explicitly organized by morphology.
techniques.applicability: Directly compatible with your LoRA contrastive fine-tune: add a small tagging or feature-contrastive head on top of the morph channel, weight it low, and ablate it. This is the mechanism by which morphology enters the *representation* rather than the tokenizer.
techniques.evidence: Cotterell & Schütze, NAACL 2015 (log-bilinear model extended with morphologically annotated data, German case study); analogous multi-task framing in Akdemir, Shibuya & Güngör (arXiv 2004.12247), which reports +18.86 F1 (DEP) and +4.61 F1 (NER) for Turkish under hierarchical multi-task learning.

techniques.name: Morpheme-indexed tensorized embedding table
techniques.description: Build the embedding table over morphemes rather than words, composing word vectors as tensor products of morpheme vectors, so parameters scale with the (small) morpheme inventory.
techniques.applicability: Attractive if you want the morph channel to be genuinely tiny. Turkish has a bounded suffix inventory (~120-130 productive suffixes in Zemberek per your project notes), so a morpheme-indexed table is small by construction.
techniques.evidence: MorphTE (arXiv 2210.15379): abstract reports ~20x word-embedding compression without performance loss on four translation datasets, outperforming other compression methods.

techniques.name: Tokenizer surgery + offline distillation to de-fragment Turkish
techniques.description: Prune a multilingual teacher's vocabulary, rebuild a Turkish-heavy vocabulary, re-initialize the embedding table by mean-composition of old token vectors, keep the transformer backbone, then distill from precomputed teacher embeddings with a cosine objective.
techniques.applicability: A strong ablation arm and possibly a pre-step for your semantic encoder: it isolates 'Turkish fragmentation is the problem' from 'the model lacks morphological representation'. If surgery alone closes most of your morph-eval gap, the second channel is not earning its keep.
techniques.evidence: Bayram, Diri & Yıldırım (arXiv 2605.29992): ~200M student reaches STSb-TR 77.55/77.45 Pearson/Spearman vs the ~300M teacher's 73.84/72.92; TR-MTEB mean 63.9%.

techniques.name: Layerwise morphological probing before committing to a second channel
techniques.description: Train linear probes to recover morphological tags (case, number, tense, negation, possession) from each layer of the candidate semantic encoder.
techniques.applicability: Run this during model selection. If Turkish morphological features are already linearly decodable from your chosen semantic encoder's mid layers, the cheaper design is a morphology-aware *pooling/objective* change, not a separate encoder. This directly informs your Section C probe and your architecture decision.
techniques.evidence: Morphosyntactic probing of multilingual BERT models (Natural Language Engineering); general finding in that literature that morphological information is recoverable and layer-dependent. I saw summary-level claims only, no numbers.

techniques.name: Late interaction as the competing baseline for morphological matching
techniques.description: ColBERT-style token-level MaxSim scoring instead of a single pooled vector, which lets individual Turkish subword tokens match across query and document.
techniques.applicability: Not a morphology technique per se, but the architecture you must beat. Late interaction already recovers much of the sub-lexical matching a morphology channel is meant to add, and does it with fewer parameters on Turkish. Include a Turkish ColBERT model in your comparison or the two-channel claim will be contestable.
techniques.evidence: TurkColBERT (arXiv 2511.16528): abstract reports late-interaction models 3-5x smaller significantly outperforming dense encoders on five Turkish BEIR datasets; colbert-hash-nano-tr (1.0M params) retains >71% of turkish-e5-large's (600M) average mAP; ColmmBERT-base-TR up to +13.8% mAP on domain-specific tasks.

techniques.name: Derivational/dual-route segmentation for semantic generalization
techniques.description: Feed the encoder a morpheme-respecting segmentation and treat the model as a serial dual-route system: frequent complex words are stored whole, novel ones composed from morphemes.
techniques.applicability: This is the theoretical justification for your two-channel split — one channel stores lexical-semantic content, one composes morphological structure. Cite it when motivating the architecture, and consider a gating/routing mechanism (frequent forms → semantic channel, rare/novel inflected forms → morph channel) rather than fixed-weight fusion.
techniques.evidence: Hofmann, Pierrehumbert & Schütze, ACL 2021 ('Superbizarre'): DelBERT with derivational segmentation reported to substantially outperform WordPiece BERT on semantic probing of complex words. English-only.

techniques.name: Intrinsic segmentation diagnostics as model-selection features
techniques.description: Score each candidate encoder's tokenizer against gold Turkish morpheme boundaries: boundary micro/macro-F1, lemma atomicity vs surface boundary hits, over-/under-segmentation indices, affix-type coverage, continuation rate, tokens-per-word fertility.
techniques.applicability: Cheap to compute, needs no GPU, and slots straight into your Section E weighted selection matrix as a morphology column that is independent of the 50-triplet probe. Also useful for sanity-checking a synthetically generated eval set: if the LLM-generated negatives are not actually single-morpheme perturbations, boundary diagnostics will show it.
techniques.evidence: Altinok (arXiv 2602.06942) proposes this diagnostic toolkit; MorphBPE (arXiv 2502.00894) contributes Morphological Consistency F1 and Morphological Edit Distance; Morpheus reports MorphScore macro-F1 (0.61 vs ~0.32 for subword).

gaps: No paper I found builds and evaluates an explicit two-channel (semantic + morphological) dual-encoder for retrieval in an agglutinative language. The closest are Morpheus (morphology-aware embedder evaluated on lexical retrieval probes, not a deployed dual encoder) and gated fusion of contextual embeddings with morphological features for Kazakh lexical complexity prediction — a classification task, not retrieval. Your architecture appears to be genuinely underexplored; that is an opportunity but also means no published fusion recipe (concatenation vs gating vs score-level interpolation vs learned routing) to copy.

The Turkish tokenization evidence is contradictory and unresolved. Toraman et al. (TALLIP) found morphological tokenization only competitive with BPE/WordPiece on Turkish downstream tasks, while Morpheus, 'Tokens with Meaning' and MorphBPE report clear gains. The discrepancy is confounded by vocabulary size, model scale and task choice — Toraman et al. specifically note morphological tokenizers benefit more from larger vocabularies, so several comparisons may be at unfavourable vocabulary budgets. Do not cite either side as settled.

Almost no work isolates morphology at the *retrieval* stage. Nearly everything measures LM loss, STS, NER, POS, dependency parsing or word similarity. The only Turkish morphology-adjacent retrieval numbers I found are HeceTokenizer's Recall@5 on TQuAD (50.3% vs 46.92%, syllable vs a morphology-driven baseline, tiny model) and TurkColBERT's mAP figures (which do not analyse morphology). Your 50-query typed-negative eval set is filling a real hole.

Adapters/LoRA carrying specifically *morphological* signal is a gap I could not fill. I found language adapters, language-family adapters, prefix-based cross-lingual transfer and knowledge-graph adapters, but no paper that trains an adapter or LoRA module with a morphological objective and measures morphological sensitivity. If such work exists it did not surface in six varied queries. Treat 'morphological LoRA' as your own contribution, not a replication.

No evidence found on whether LLM-synthesized morphological hard negatives are reliable for agglutinative languages. The hard-negative literature I found (HNCSE, focal-InfoNCE, mixup negatives) is general-purpose sentence-embedding work with no morphological typing. Before scaling your eval set with an LLM, plan a validation pass: verify each generated negative really differs by the intended single morphological feature (a morphological analyzer can check this automatically).

Provenance risk on the very recent Turkish arXiv preprints. Morpheus (2606.18717), HeceTokenizer (2604.10665), the Turkish tokenizer-surgery paper (2605.29992) and Altinok's subword-strategies paper (2602.06942) are all 2026 preprints, several apparently single-author and none obviously peer-reviewed. I verified the first three exist by fetching their arXiv pages, but their headline numbers (e.g. same-root ROC-AUC 1.00) are self-reported and unreplicated. Weight them accordingly in a selection matrix.

Finnish, Hungarian, Estonian and Basque are thinly covered here. Hungarian appears only inside MorphBPE's four-language set; Finnish appears only in a Word2Vec tokenization case study I did not read; Estonian and Basque did not surface at all. If you want cross-language corroboration that a morphology channel helps, that literature needs its own search pass.
confidence: Medium-high on the classic foundations, medium on the recent Turkish work, low on anything I marked search_snippet_only. Specifically: I ran 10 web searches (English and Turkish) and fetched 7 primary pages. I fetched and read abstract pages for Morpheus (2606.18717), TurkColBERT (2511.16528), Toraman et al. (2204.08832), Akdemir et al. (2004.12247), HeceTokenizer (2604.10665), Tokens with Meaning (2508.14292), tokenizer surgery (2605.29992) and MorphBPE (2502.00894) — every number I attribute to those is from the abstract/landing page, NOT from result tables in the full PDF, so I could not check experimental conditions, baselines-at-matched-scale, or statistical significance for any of them. Everything cited for Bojanowski 2017, Luong et al. 2013, Kim et al. 2016, Cotterell & Schütze 2015, Superbizarre, MorphTE, MorphPiece, the Korean tokenization work and the morphosyntactic-probing article comes from search-result summaries only; titles/authors/venues for those are standard and I am confident in them, but I did not verify their numbers and have deliberately reported few. Three specific caveats: (1) the Morpheus fetch summary asserted 'confirmed dual-encoding capability' — that phrasing is the fetcher's inference, not a claim I saw the paper make; the paper reports lexical-retrieval MAP and same-root ROC-AUC, which is not the same as a working dual-encoder retrieval system. (2) HeceTokenizer's '200x larger morphology-driven baseline' is as stated on the abstract page; I could not identify which model that was. (3) I could not confirm the author list or year for the Cambridge morphosyntactic-probing article and left those null. No paper, author, number or venue in this report was invented; where I was unsure I set the field to null or flagged it in gaps.

topic: Eval-set design: building and validating benchmarks that isolate a single linguistic feature, and using LLMs to synthesize them (minimal pairs, contrast/counterfactual sets, CheckList, synthetic IR data generation, and the QC machinery around all of it)

papers.title: BLiMP: The Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for English
papers.why_relevant: The canonical template for 'isolate one linguistic contrast, 1000 items per paradigm' benchmark design, and the source of the crowd-validation protocol that most later minimal-pair sets copy. Directly transferable QC recipe for a morphology-isolating eval set.
papers.approach: 67 paradigms x 1000 sentence pairs, grouped into 12 phenomena. Fully synthetic generation from linguist-crafted grammar templates; lexical items sampled from a hand-annotated vocabulary of >3,000 items carrying morphological/syntactic/semantic features to enforce selectional restrictions (11 verb subcategorization frames). Pairs are matched for length (length defined as number of lexicon entries) and reuse the same verb phrase + arguments across both members of a pair, so probability differences are attributable to the intended contrast. Paper explicitly notes LM probability is only a valid acceptability proxy if length and lexical content are controlled.
papers.key_results: Human validation via Amazon Mechanical Turk: 20 validators x 5 pairs from each of 67 paradigms = 6,700 forced-choice judgments; gold = majority vote. Aggregate human agreement with BLiMP labels 96.4%; individual human agreement 88.6%. Inclusion rule: a majority of validators had to agree with BLiMP on at least 4/5 sampled examples for the paradigm to be included; all 67 released paradigms passed, 2 additional paradigms were rejected on this criterion. Each HIT contained an attention-check item and a hidden field to catch bot-assisted workers; $0.25 per 5 judgments. Baselines: GPT-2 80.1 overall vs human 88.6; 5-gram 60.5, LSTM 68.9, Transformer-XL 68.7.

papers.title: TurBLiMP: A Turkish Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs
papers.why_relevant: The single most directly transferable paper for this project: a Turkish, morphology-and-word-order-aware minimal-pair benchmark, with an explicit hybrid manual/semi-automatic/automatic construction pipeline and a Turkish native-speaker validation study. Its phenomenon inventory (nominalization -DIK/-mA, suspended affixation, subject agreement, NPI licensing, irregular aorist allomorphs, relative clauses, scrambling) is close to a ready-made typology for morphological hard negatives.
papers.approach: Three-fold pipeline. (1) 10 samples per phenomenon crafted entirely manually to establish guidelines and guarantee each pair differs only minimally. (2) Semi-automatic augmentation: masked Turkish LM BERTurk suggests lexical replacements at random positions; every replacement verified and adjusted manually -> 100 validated pairs per phenomenon. (3) Fully automated augmentation: BERTurk proposes contextually appropriate replacement words, then the Turkish morphology pipeline of Akın & Akın (2007) re-inflects them with the same morphological features -> 1000 pairs per phenomenon. Separately, 'experimental paradigms' derive all 6 subject/verb/object orders and 4 subordination structures for the Transitive and Ditransitive Argument Structure phenomena, adding 2,000 pairs on top of the 16,000 base.
papers.key_results: 16 phenomena x 1000 pairs = 16,000, plus 2,000 paradigm pairs. Human validation: 30 native Turkish speakers (17 linguistics students, 13 non-linguists), 7-point Likert (1 completely unacceptable – 7 completely acceptable), anonymous online survey; each participant rated 216 sentences covering 16 phenomena + 20 experimental paradigms, with 3 acceptable and 3 unacceptable sentences per category and the acceptability conditions flipped between two survey versions. Likert ratings z-score-normalized per participant. Island Effects (Δ1.00), Passives (Δ1.06), Nominalization (Δ1.15) were the least discriminable phenomena; Suspended Affixation most (Δ2.14). 13 LMs evaluated by full-sequence log-probability (minicons); model average 63.3–93.7. Only BERTurk correlated significantly with human judgments across phenomena (Pearson r = 0.65, p = 0.007). SLOR (Pauls & Klein 2012) used as a length/frequency-normalized alternative metric to rule out metric artifacts. Appendix E reports a surface-confound analysis of sentence length and subword counts; authors note acceptable sentences are consistently shorter than unacceptable ones in some paradigms.

papers.title: A Morphology-Aware Evaluation of Turkish Syntax in Large Language Models
papers.venue: SIGTURK 2026 (Second Workshop on NLP for Turkic Languages), pp. 95–102
papers.why_relevant: Explicitly about the confounders that a Turkish morphology-isolating eval set must audit for. This is the paper to imitate when writing the 'we checked our eval set for artifacts' section.
papers.approach: Analyses how surface-level factors — morpheme count, subword count, sentence length — and the alignment between tokenizer boundaries and morphological boundaries relate to LM performance on Turkish minimal-pair benchmarks.
papers.key_results: Abstract states surface factors have limited predictive power but may still act as a systematic source of bias, that morphological alignment corresponds with model performance, and that morpheme-level imbalances in a benchmark may significantly influence evaluation results. No specific numbers were visible on the landing page.

papers.title: MultiBLiMP 1.0: A Massively Multilingual Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs
papers.why_relevant: Shows the alternative to hand-written templates: derive minimal pairs automatically from existing morphological resources. For Turkish this is the cheapest route to scale — UD trees give the syntactic frame, UniMorph gives the paradigm cell to perturb, so the perturbation is guaranteed to be a single feature change rather than an LLM's guess.
papers.approach: Fully automated pipeline that combines Universal Dependencies treebanks with UniMorph inflection tables to construct subject-verb agreement minimal pairs; no per-language grammar engineering.
papers.key_results: Reported as covering 101 languages, 2 types of subject-verb agreement, and more than 128,000 minimal pairs. I did not read the full text, so I have not verified per-language counts or any validation statistics.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList
papers.why_relevant: Gives the test typology that maps almost one-to-one onto typed hard negatives: an item where a suffix change must flip relevance is a Directional Expectation test; an item where an orthographic/stylistic change must NOT change relevance is an Invariance test; a simple single-suffix probe is a Minimum Functionality Test. Useful for justifying and naming the negative types in an eval set.
papers.approach: A capability x test-type matrix (capabilities such as vocabulary, negation, coreference, logic; test types MFT / INV / DIR) plus templating tooling to mass-produce test cases from a small number of templates and fill-in lexicons.
papers.key_results: Reported user study: practitioners using CheckList created about twice as many tests and found roughly three times as many bugs as those without it. I saw these as search-result claims, not in the fetched paper.

papers.title: Evaluating Models' Local Decision Boundaries via Contrast Sets
papers.why_relevant: The methodological argument for exactly the eval set this project already has: a held-out set of expert-authored minimal perturbations around each seed item, evaluated separately from the in-distribution test set. Also the source of the 'contrast consistency' framing (score a seed as correct only if the model gets the whole cluster right), which is a much harsher and more informative metric than mean nDCG over a synthetic set.
papers.approach: After a dataset exists, dataset authors (not crowdworkers) manually perturb test instances in small, meaningful ways that usually change the gold label, producing a contrast set that probes the model's local decision boundary.
papers.key_results: Contrast sets built for 10 diverse NLP datasets (incl. DROP, UD parsing, IMDb); model performance dropped substantially versus original test sets — reported as up to about 25 points in some cases. Number seen in search results only.

papers.title: Learning the Difference that Makes a Difference with Counterfactually-Augmented Data
papers.why_relevant: Source of the three editing constraints that should be handed verbatim to an LLM generating morphological counterfactuals: the edit must (i) accord with the counterfactual target label, (ii) retain internal coherence, (iii) avoid unnecessary changes. Constraint (iii) is exactly what stops an LLM from rewriting the whole sentence when only a suffix should change.
papers.approach: Humans revise documents to flip the gold label under those three constraints, producing paired original/counterfactual data for sentiment and NLI.
papers.key_results: Classifiers trained on original data fail on counterfactually-revised counterparts and vice versa; training on the combined set is nearly as good as specializing to either. I did not read the full text and have no verified numbers.

papers.title: Misleading Failures of Partial-input Baselines
papers.why_relevant: The standard artifact-detection tool, and a warning about over-reading it. For a retrieval eval set the analogue is a query-only / candidate-only / BM25-only baseline: if a lexical-overlap-only scorer can pick the gold from the typed negatives, the item is solvable for the wrong reason and either the negatives or the gold need rebalancing.
papers.approach: Restrict a model to part of the input; high accuracy implies the dataset is solvable via unintended patterns. The paper also argues that a failing partial-input baseline does not prove a dataset is artifact-free, so it should be treated as hypothesis testing rather than certification.

papers.title: InPars-v2: Large Language Models as Efficient Dataset Generators for Information Retrieval
papers.authors_short: Jeronymo, Bonifacio, Abonizio, Fadaee, Lotufo, Zavrel, Nogueira
papers.why_relevant: The cleanest example of model-based post-hoc filtering of LLM-generated query/passage pairs — the same trick works for filtering LLM-synthesized morphological eval items (score every candidate with a strong reranker, keep only items where the intended gold actually wins by a margin, and inspect the ones where it does not).
papers.approach: Open-source LLMs generate queries for documents; an existing powerful reranker (a monoT5 reranker finetuned on InPars data) scores and selects the synthetic query-document pairs kept for training. Successor to InPars (fixed prompt) and contemporary of Promptagator (dataset-specific prompts).
papers.key_results: Abstract claims new state-of-the-art on BEIR with a BM25 + monoT5 pipeline; code, synthetic datasets and models released. Exact nDCG@10 values were not visible in the abstract I read.

papers.title: Promptagator: Few-shot Dense Retrieval From 8 Examples
papers.why_relevant: Round-trip consistency filtering is the single most reusable QC mechanism for synthetic retrieval data: keep a generated query only if a retriever trained on the synthetic data retrieves the source passage back. For an eval set it doubles as a double-gold detector — if the round-trip retrieves a *different* passage above the intended gold, that passage is a candidate false negative.
papers.approach: Dataset-specific prompt templates with 2–8 examples generate task-specific queries per corpus; an initial retriever trained on the raw synthetic data then filters queries that fail to retrieve their own source passage.
papers.key_results: Reported: outperforms ColBERT v2 by more than 1.2 nDCG on average over 11 retrieval sets; reranker trained on the same data adds ~5.0 nDCG; consistency filtering helps 8 of 11 datasets for ~2.5 points average gain. Numbers seen in search results, not verified in the PDF.

papers.title: Improving Text Embeddings with Large Language Models (E5-mistral)
papers.why_relevant: Source of the two-step 'brainstorm task templates, then instantiate' prompting pattern, which is the main defence against degenerate templates when an LLM is asked to synthesize thousands of eval items. Also the reference point for how much synthetic-only data can carry an embedding model.
papers.approach: Proprietary LLMs (GPT-3.5-Turbo / GPT-4, roughly 25% / 75% split per the snippet) first brainstorm a pool of embedding-task templates, then generate the actual (query, positive, hard negative) instances for each template, with explicit variation slots. Mistral-7B is then contrastively finetuned on a mix of synthetic and ~13 public labeled datasets (~1.8M examples).
papers.key_results: Reported: E5-mistral-7b with full data tops MTEB by 2.4 points over the prior SOTA at the time; synthetic-data-only remains competitive. Numbers from search results, not verified in the fetched paper.

papers.title: Gecko: Versatile Text Embeddings Distilled from Large Language Models
papers.why_relevant: Introduces LLM *relabeling* as a distinct QC stage: after generating a query from a passage, retrieve candidates and let the LLM re-decide which candidate is the true positive and which are hard negatives. This is the mechanism most likely to catch the 'double gold' failure mode in a synthesized morphological eval set, where a distractor accidentally satisfies the query better than the intended gold.
papers.approach: Two-step distillation: (1) LLM generates diverse synthetic paired data; (2) for each query, retrieve a candidate set from the corpus and have the same LLM relabel the positive and the hard negatives, so the seed passage is not automatically assumed to be the best positive.
papers.key_results: Reported: Gecko at 256 dims beats all prior 768-dim MTEB entries; 768-dim Gecko averages 66.31 on MTEB. Numbers from search results only.

papers.title: Leveraging LLMs for Synthesizing Training Data Across Many Languages in Multilingual Dense Retrieval (SWIM-IR)
papers.language_focus: Multilingual, 33 languages (Turkish included in the SWIM-IR language set)
papers.why_relevant: The closest large-scale precedent for generating retrieval data in a non-English morphologically rich language with an LLM, and a cautionary data point on QC: the authors report that hallucinated queries occur but argue they did not materially hurt retrieval effectiveness — a claim worth testing rather than inheriting, since an *eval* set is far less tolerant of hallucination than a *training* set.
papers.approach: Summarize-then-ask prompting (SAP): the prompt contains the passage plus a human-written summary so the LLM first localizes the relevant span, then asks a question about it; 5-shot exemplars for cross-lingual, 3-shot for monolingual generation, using PaLM 2. Cross-lingual variants use MT-translated seed questions.
papers.key_results: Reported: 28M query-passage pairs over 33 languages; SWIM-X beats the best supervised cross-lingual baseline by 7.1 Recall@5kt on XOR-Retrieve. Numbers from search results only.

papers.title: Silencer: From Discovery to Mitigation of Self-Bias in LLM-as-Benchmark-Generator
papers.why_relevant: Directly answers 'what goes wrong when an LLM builds your eval set'. Decomposes self-bias into question-domain bias, language-style bias, and wrong labels, and shows that explicit diversity instructions in the prompt are not sufficient — stylistic homogeneity persists and inflates the generator family's own scores. Practical implication: do not generate the Turkish morph eval set with the same model family you intend to benchmark or to use as judge.
papers.approach: Measures inflation of a model's score on benchmarks it generated itself; mitigation uses multiple heterogeneous LLM generators and aggregates at both the sample level and the benchmark level to cancel generator-specific bias.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports Pearson correlation with a high-quality human-annotated benchmark rising from 0.655 to 0.833 after applying Silencer, and self-bias suppressed to near zero. Related work in the same search (Preference Leakage, arXiv 2502.01534) documents judges favouring models sharing lineage with the data generator.

papers.title: NV-Retriever: Improving text embedding models with effective hard-negative mining
papers.authors_short: Moreira, Osmulski, Xu, Ak, Schifferer, Oldridge
papers.why_relevant: Gives a concrete, threshold-based rule for rejecting a candidate hard negative that is probably a false negative, anchored on the positive's own relevance score. This is exactly the automated screen needed to keep synthesized 'partial_trap' / 'same_feature_wrong_content' candidates from silently being second golds.
papers.approach: Positive-aware hard-negative mining: use the teacher score of the known positive as an anchor and discard mined negatives whose score is too close to (or above) it, rather than blindly taking top-k nearest neighbours.
papers.key_results: Abstract reports NV-Retriever-v1 scoring 60.9 on MTEB Retrieval (BEIR) and ranking 1st at time of publication (July 2024). I did not verify the exact percentage-of-positive thresholds or the ablation table.

techniques.name: Three-stage seed → semi-automatic → automatic augmentation (with a human gate in the middle)
techniques.description: TurBLiMP's construction pattern: hand-write ~10 items per phenomenon to fix the guideline, then expand to ~100 by proposing lexical substitutions with a masked LM where every substitution is manually verified, then expand to 1000 fully automatically once the substitution recipe is proven. The manual middle stage is what makes the final automatic stage trustworthy.
techniques.applicability: Map directly onto the plan to scale the 50-query set with an LLM: freeze the current 50 reviewed queries as the seed layer, LLM-expand to a few hundred with 100% human review, and only then let the LLM run unattended — and report the three tiers separately so a reviewer can see which items were human-checked.
techniques.evidence: TurBLiMP §4.2 (Başar et al., EMNLP 2025): 10 manual samples per phenomenon → 100 manually validated pairs → 1000 pairs per phenomenon.

techniques.name: Morphological re-inflection of substituted lexical items
techniques.description: When a generator swaps a content word into a template, run the replacement through a morphological analyzer/generator and re-apply the *same* morphological feature bundle, so the substitution cannot accidentally alter the feature under test.
techniques.applicability: Essential for Turkish: an LLM that swaps a noun into a slot will often get vowel harmony, buffer consonants or case stacking wrong, silently converting a morph_counterfactual into a plain typo. Running Zemberek (or equivalent) as a post-generation normalizer, and rejecting any item the analyzer cannot parse, is a cheap high-yield filter.
techniques.evidence: TurBLiMP used the Turkish morphology pipeline of Akın & Akın (2007) to inflect BERTurk-proposed replacements with the same morphological features where applicable.

techniques.name: Forced-choice validation with a paradigm-level pass/fail threshold
techniques.description: Have humans do the *same* task the model does (pick the correct member from the pair/cluster), take majority vote as gold, and then drop an entire item type if humans do not reproduce the intended label on a required fraction of sampled items.
techniques.applicability: Adapt as: sample k items per negative type, ask 3–5 native Turkish speakers to pick the gold passage from the ~11 candidates, and retire a negative type whose human accuracy falls below the threshold — rather than patching individual items. This catches systematically broken negative types (a 'partial_trap' template that is actually ambiguous) instead of one-off noise.
techniques.evidence: BLiMP §3.4: 20 validators x 5 pairs per paradigm (6,700 judgments); paradigm included only if a majority agreed with the label on ≥4/5 sampled items; 2 paradigms rejected; aggregate agreement 96.4%, individual agreement 88.6%.

techniques.name: Graded Likert judgments + per-participant z-scoring + discriminability screen
techniques.description: Instead of (or alongside) forced choice, collect 7-point acceptability/relevance ratings, z-score per participant to normalize scale use, and compute the mean gap between intended-good and intended-bad items per phenomenon. Small gaps flag phenomena that are not perceptible even to native speakers.
techniques.applicability: Gives a per-negative-type difficulty calibration for the Turkish set. If e.g. 'state_variant' shows a small human gap, low model scores on it are not evidence of a morphology failure — the same trap TurBLiMP identified for Island Effects, Passives and Nominalization.
techniques.evidence: TurBLiMP §5: 30 native speakers, 7-point Likert, 216 sentences each, 3 acceptable + 3 unacceptable per category, conditions flipped between two survey versions, Likert → z-scores; Island Effects Δ1.00 vs Suspended Affixation Δ2.14.

techniques.name: Human–model correlation as a benchmark validity check
techniques.description: Correlate per-phenomenon model scores against per-phenomenon human ratings. A benchmark where no model tracks humans at all is either measuring something else or is dominated by artifacts.
techniques.applicability: Report Pearson r between human difficulty and model difficulty across the typed negative categories as a headline validity statistic for the synthesized Turkish set; it is a much stronger claim than 'we collected 500 items'.
techniques.evidence: TurBLiMP Fig. 2: BERTurk r = 0.65, p = 0.007 across 16 phenomena; none of the other 12 models showed a statistically significant correlation in either direction.

techniques.name: Length, frequency and tokenization confound audit
techniques.description: Explicitly measure whether gold and negatives differ systematically in surface properties — token length, subword count, morpheme count, tokenizer/morpheme boundary alignment — and either balance them or report the imbalance. Use a length/frequency-normalized scoring variant (e.g. SLOR) as a robustness check that results are not a scoring artifact.
techniques.applicability: For a Turkish morph retrieval set this is the highest-risk artifact: a morph_counterfactual is usually one suffix longer or shorter than the gold, and subword tokenizers split Turkish suffixes inconsistently, so 'morphological sensitivity' can be silently confounded with 'sensitivity to sequence length'. Bucket the eval set by morpheme-count delta and report scores per bucket.
techniques.evidence: BLiMP matches pair length by lexicon-entry count and warns that LM probability is only a valid proxy if length and lexical content are controlled; TurBLiMP adds a SLOR check and a subword/length confound analysis (Appendix E) and notes acceptable sentences were consistently shorter; Başar & Bisazza (SIGTURK 2026) analyse morpheme count, subword count, length and tokenizer-morphology alignment as systematic bias sources.

techniques.name: Fraud/attention controls in crowd validation
techniques.description: Embed attention-check items and bot-detection traps in every annotation batch, and drop annotators who fail them, before computing any agreement statistic.
techniques.applicability: Necessary if the Turkish validation is crowdsourced rather than done by the project's own reviewers; cheap to add and it is what makes a 96%-agreement number credible.
techniques.evidence: BLiMP §3.4: each HIT included an attention-check item and a hidden field question to catch bot-assisted humans; a few annotators were excluded as ineligible.

techniques.name: CheckList test typology (MFT / INV / DIR) as the schema for typed negatives
techniques.description: Classify each item by the *expected behavioural response* rather than by surface construction: MFT = simplest possible probe of one capability; INV = perturbation that must not change the prediction; DIR = perturbation that must change it in a specified direction.
techniques.applicability: Gives principled names and, more importantly, principled *pass conditions* for the existing negative types: morph_counterfactual is a DIR item (gold must lose), state_variant is arguably an INV item (ranking should be stable), partial_trap is an MFT. Items whose type does not imply a clear expected direction are the ones most likely to be badly formed.
techniques.evidence: Ribeiro et al., ACL 2020, capability x test-type matrix.

techniques.name: Contrast-cluster scoring (contrast consistency) rather than mean metric
techniques.description: Group every generated item with its seed and score the model as correct only if it handles the entire cluster — original plus all perturbations — correctly. Mean nDCG over a synthetic set hides the case where a model wins on easy clusters and fails every hard perturbation.
techniques.applicability: Since the eval set already has one gold plus several typed negatives per query, a natural per-query metric is 'gold ranked above every typed negative', reported alongside nDCG@10 and broken out per negative type.
techniques.evidence: Gardner et al. (Findings EMNLP 2020) introduced contrast sets as a local decision-boundary probe; reported drops of up to ~25 points versus original test sets (search-result claim).

techniques.name: Minimal-edit constraints in the generation prompt
techniques.description: Instruct the generator that the edited item must (i) satisfy the target label, (ii) remain internally coherent, and (iii) avoid unnecessary changes. Then enforce (iii) mechanically — reject any generation whose character/token edit distance from the seed exceeds a threshold, or that changes more than one morpheme.
techniques.applicability: This is the difference between a real morph counterfactual and a paraphrase. A programmatic diff check on the suffix chain (analyzer output before vs after) is a stricter and cheaper enforcement than trusting the LLM's self-report.
techniques.evidence: Kaushik, Hovy & Lipton (ICLR 2020) state the three revision constraints given to their human editors.

techniques.name: Partial-input / lexical-shortcut baselines on the eval set itself
techniques.description: Before trusting a new eval set, run degenerate scorers on it: BM25 or pure character n-gram overlap, query-only, candidate-only, and a lemma-stripped variant. Whatever fraction those solve is the fraction that does not require the capability you claim to measure.
techniques.applicability: Highly relevant here: Turkish suffix changes barely move surface overlap, so a BM25 baseline that scores near-perfect on the morph set means the negatives are lexically distinguishable and the set is not isolating morphology. Conversely, a stem-only (Zemberek-lemmatized) baseline that still solves items reveals items where the morphology is decorative. Report both as artifact statistics in the eval-set card.
techniques.evidence: Partial-input baseline methodology, ACL 2019 (aclanthology.org/P19-1554); the same paper cautions that a failing partial-input baseline is not proof of an artifact-free dataset.

techniques.name: Round-trip consistency filtering (and its use as a double-gold detector)
techniques.description: Train or use a retriever, feed each generated query back over the corpus, and keep the item only if the intended gold comes back at rank 1 (or within top-k). Items where a *different* passage outranks the gold are surfaced for human adjudication rather than deleted.
techniques.applicability: The cheapest automated way to find the double-gold problem in a synthesized Turkish set: if two or three independent retrievers all put a supposed hard negative above the gold, the item is ambiguous, not hard. Use an ensemble of dissimilar retrievers (BM25 + a multilingual dense model) so the filter does not simply encode one model's preferences into the benchmark.
techniques.evidence: Promptagator (Dai et al., 2022) reports consistency filtering helping 8/11 datasets for ~2.5 nDCG average (search-result numbers); InPars-v2 uses reranker-score selection for the same purpose.

techniques.name: LLM relabeling of positives and negatives after retrieval (Gecko-style)
techniques.description: Do not assume the passage that seeded the query is the best positive. Retrieve a candidate pool, then have the LLM re-rank/relabel which candidate is genuinely the positive and which are hard negatives.
techniques.applicability: Adapt as an adjudication pass: for each synthesized query, retrieve the top ~20 real Turkish passages and ask an LLM (different family from the generator) to mark every candidate as gold / hard-negative-of-type-T / irrelevant. Disagreements between the generator's intent and the relabeler's verdict are exactly the items a human reviewer should see.
techniques.evidence: Gecko (arXiv 2403.20327) two-step distillation: generate, then retrieve candidates and relabel positives and hard negatives with the same LLM.

techniques.name: Positive-anchored false-negative rejection for hard negatives
techniques.description: Rather than taking top-k nearest neighbours as negatives, threshold each candidate negative against the positive's own relevance score and discard candidates that score too close to it.
techniques.applicability: A concrete numeric screen for the typed negatives: compute a teacher score for gold and for each candidate negative, and quarantine any negative scoring above some fraction (e.g. ~95%) of the gold's score. In a benchmark, quarantine should mean human review, not silent deletion — those items are either broken or the most diagnostic ones you have.
techniques.evidence: NV-Retriever (Moreira et al., arXiv 2407.15831) positive-aware mining; I verified the concept and the headline MTEB Retrieval score of 60.9 but not the exact threshold values.

techniques.name: Two-step brainstorm-then-instantiate prompting with explicit variation axes
techniques.description: Have the LLM first generate a pool of task/template descriptions (domain, register, query length, difficulty), then generate instances conditioned on one template each, so the surface form is not drawn from a single degenerate mode.
techniques.applicability: Prevents the classic 'every synthesized Turkish query is a 6-word news-register noun phrase' failure. Pair it with a post-hoc diversity audit: n-gram/embedding-cluster entropy over the generated queries, plus a check that the generated suffix inventory actually covers the morphological features the project cares about rather than over-representing a few frequent ones.
techniques.evidence: E5-mistral (Wang et al., ACL 2024) two-step brainstorm-then-generate prompting across many task types and languages; SWIM-IR (Thakur et al., NAACL 2024) uses summarize-then-ask prompting to ground the generated query in a specific passage span.

techniques.name: Generator/judge/evaluatee family separation and multi-generator ensembling
techniques.description: Never let the same model family generate the benchmark, judge the benchmark, and be a headline evaluatee. Use several heterogeneous generators and aggregate, since explicit diversity instructions alone do not remove a generator's stylistic fingerprint.
techniques.applicability: Direct constraint on the planned LLM synthesis: if the eval set is generated with model X, models from X's family will look better on it. Since this project benchmarks multilingual embedding models from several vendors, generating with a mixture and reporting the per-generator score split is a defensible protocol.
techniques.evidence: Silencer (Yuan et al., arXiv 2505.20738) decomposes self-bias into question-domain, language-style and wrong-label components and reports human-benchmark correlation rising from 0.655 to 0.833 under multi-generator aggregation; Preference Leakage (arXiv 2502.01534) documents judge–generator lineage effects.

techniques.name: LLM-as-judge for hole patching, with its known failure mode
techniques.description: LLMs can label unjudged candidates to fill qrels holes, but they are demonstrably biased toward marking passages relevant when they share surface terms with the query — including when relevance is asserted adversarially in the text.
techniques.applicability: A serious caveat for this project specifically: if an LLM judge is used to confirm that a Turkish typed negative is truly non-relevant, its term-overlap bias will systematically mislabel the 'same_feature_wrong_content' and 'partial_trap' categories, which are engineered to share surface form with the query. Judge those two types by human review, and use the LLM judge only for the low-overlap types.
techniques.evidence: 'LLMs Can Patch Up Missing Relevance Judgments in Evaluation' (arXiv 2405.04727, Upadhyay et al., 2024) for hole-filling; 'Don't Use LLMs to Make Relevance Judgments' (arXiv 2409.15133) reports that injecting query terms, or an explicit assertion of relevance, can flip an LLM's judgment. Both seen as search results / abstract-level, not read in full.

techniques.name: Contamination hygiene for a held-out eval set
techniques.description: Keep the eval set out of any training mixture, avoid publishing it in plain scrapeable text if it is meant to stay held out, and be aware that n-gram overlap checks miss LLM-paraphrased leakage.
techniques.applicability: The morph eval set is described as held-out and will judge a LoRA-finetuned model — so any synthetic *training* data generated with the same prompts, seeds or source passages is a contamination vector even without literal string overlap. Generate training and eval items from disjoint source corpora and disjoint seed queries.
techniques.evidence: General finding across the LLM-benchmark-pitfalls literature surfaced in search (contaminated rephrasings undetectable by n-gram methods; dynamic benchmarks such as LatestEval reported at ~10% unfaithful/unanswerable generated samples on human inspection). I did not read these sources in full — treat as directional, not citable numbers.

gaps: I found no published Turkish eval set that isolates morphology for *retrieval* (dual-encoder / ranking). TurBLiMP is the closest resource but it is an LM log-probability acceptability benchmark over sentence pairs, not a query/candidate ranking set — so this project's 50-query typed-hard-negative set appears to have no direct published analogue, and its construction protocol will have to be argued from BLiMP/TurBLiMP + contrast-set methodology rather than cited from a Turkish predecessor.

No paper I found validates *generative-LLM*-synthesized minimal pairs for Turkish morphology. TurBLiMP deliberately used a masked LM (BERTurk) for lexical substitution plus a rule-based morphological analyzer for re-inflection, with human verification, rather than an instruction-tuned LLM. Whether an LLM can produce well-formed Turkish morphological counterfactuals at scale is, as far as this search goes, an open question — which argues for a measured human-audit rate on the first synthesis batch.

I could not verify exact numbers for several abstract-level sources: InPars-v2's nDCG@10 values and synthetic-pair counts, Gecko's full pipeline details, SWIM-IR's hallucination-rate measurement, NV-Retriever's specific percentage-of-positive thresholds, and Silencer's per-sub-bias magnitudes. The Promptagator (+2.5 nDCG, 8/11 datasets), CheckList (2x tests, 3x bugs), Gardner (up to ~25 point drop) and E5-mistral (+2.4 MTEB) figures come from search-result summaries, not from pages I fetched — they should be re-checked against the PDFs before appearing in a write-up.

Turkish-language search terms ('morfolojik değerlendirme kümesi', 'minimal çift') returned essentially nothing usable — the relevant Turkish NLP eval-design literature appears to be published in English at ACL venues. Turkish-language querying is not a productive channel for this topic.

There is no standard, agreed-upon metric for 'contrast consistency' in *retrieval* the way there is for classification/QA. The project will likely have to define its own (e.g. fraction of queries where gold outranks every typed negative, plus per-type breakdown) and defend it.

Double-gold / ambiguity detection in retrieval eval sets is handled in the literature only indirectly — via false-negative filtering during hard-negative mining (NV-Retriever), round-trip consistency (Promptagator), LLM relabeling (Gecko), and qrels hole-patching (Upadhyay et al.). I found no paper that treats 'is this hard negative accidentally a second gold?' as a first-class benchmark-QC problem with a validated protocol.

I did not verify CLiMP (Chinese) or the other BLiMP analogues (ZhoBLiMP, BLiMP-NL, JBLiMP, RuBLiMP, Icelandic, Basque/Swahili/Hindi) beyond their appearance in TurBLiMP's related-work section. BLiMP-NL is noted there as the source of the Likert-scale validation approach TurBLiMP adopted, and Leong et al. (2023) is cited there as using LLMs to generate pairs for Tamil and Indonesian — that last one is probably the most relevant uncited-here lead for LLM-generated minimal pairs and is worth a follow-up.
confidence: Medium-high overall, with clearly uneven per-item confidence. High confidence in everything reported for BLiMP and TurBLiMP: I read both full PDFs and the numbers quoted (6,700 validation judgments, 96.4%/88.6% agreement, the 4/5 paradigm inclusion rule, 2 rejected paradigms; TurBLiMP's 30 annotators, 7-point Likert, 216 items each, 16x1000 + 2000 pairs, the 10→100→1000 pipeline, BERTurk r=0.65 p=0.007, the SLOR and subword-confound checks) were read directly off the pages. Medium confidence on the abstract-level entries (InPars-v2, Silencer, NV-Retriever, Başar & Bisazza SIGTURK 2026) — claims are accurate to the abstracts I fetched but I did not see the methods sections. Lower confidence on the search-snippet-only entries (Promptagator, E5-mistral, Gecko, SWIM-IR, CheckList, Gardner, Kaushik, MultiBLiMP, the partial-input baselines paper): titles/venues/URLs are real and appeared in results, but the quantitative claims come from search summaries and should be verified against the PDFs before citation. Author lists I could not confirm are set to null rather than guessed. I ran 12 searches and fetched/read 5 primary sources (2 in full).

topic: morph-ir — Information retrieval for morphologically rich languages, and morphological sensitivity in dense retrieval (with a Turkish focus)

papers.title: Information Retrieval on Turkish Texts
papers.venue: JASIST (Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology)
papers.approach: Built a large Turkish ad-hoc test collection (Milliyet newspaper) and compared indexing units: no stemming, simple fixed-length word truncation (prefix-n, notably first-5 / 'F5'), corpus-statistics-driven truncation, and an elaborate lemmatizer-based stemmer, crossed with several query-document matching functions.
papers.key_results: Collection reported as 408,305 documents and 72 ad hoc queries. The headline claim I saw repeated is that simple prefix truncation, statistics-based truncation, and a lemmatizer-based stemmer give *similar* retrieval effectiveness, with truncation at prefix length 5 being an effective indexing choice. One snippet also stated the lemmatizer-based stemmer was significantly better across matching functions — these two framings conflict and I could not open the full text to adjudicate.
papers.why_relevant: The canonical reference point for 'how much does morphological normalization actually buy you in Turkish IR'. It is the baseline every morphology-aware Turkish retrieval claim gets measured against, and it establishes that crude prefix truncation is a surprisingly strong lexical baseline — worth including as a sparse baseline in the dual-encoder project.

papers.title: Comparison of Different Lemmatization Approaches for Information Retrieval on Turkish Text Collection
papers.venue: IEEE conference (INISTA-style venue; exact year not confirmed)
papers.approach: Head-to-head comparison of lemmatization / stemming strategies for Turkish IR on a Turkish text collection.
papers.why_relevant: Second data point on the classical stemming-vs-lemmatization question for Turkish; useful for the related-work framing of 'why a learned morphological channel instead of a rule-based analyzer'.

papers.title: Stemming and N-gram Matching for Term Conflation in Turkish Texts
papers.approach: Compares rule-based stemming against character n-gram matching as term-conflation strategies for Turkish retrieval.
papers.why_relevant: The classical argument for character n-gram indexing in agglutinative IR — the direct ancestor of 'let subword/character signal do the morphology for you'. Relevant if the morphological channel encoder ends up being character/n-gram based.

papers.title: Stemming in Agglutinative Languages: A Probabilistic Stemmer for Turkish
papers.approach: A lexicon-free probabilistic stemmer for Turkish IR with linear computational complexity.
papers.key_results: Reported test success ratio of 95.8% (per search snippet, not verified in full text).
papers.why_relevant: Shows the lexicon-free statistical route to Turkish morphology — cheap, and a plausible weak-supervision source for generating morphological training signal without Zemberek-style analyzers.

papers.title: TR-MTEB: A Comprehensive Benchmark and Embedding Model Suite for Turkish Sentence Representations
papers.approach: 26 datasets across six task families (classification, clustering, pair classification, retrieval, bitext mining, STS), largely translated resources plus native ones. Also releases a 34.2M weakly-supervised Turkish sentence-pair corpus and two Turkish embedding models trained by contrastive pretraining + supervised fine-tuning.
papers.key_results: Abstract claims the released Turkish models are competitive across most tasks and substantially improve over baseline monolingual models. I did not get per-model nDCG@10 numbers — the PDF fetch returned binary and the landing page only carries the abstract.
papers.why_relevant: This is the benchmark whose retrieval subset (the `trmteb` HF org: scifact-tr, nfcorpus-tr, arguana-tr, fiqa-tr, msmarco-tr, quora-tr) the project already uses. Note for the report: the ACL landing page contains no explicit morphology discussion — TR-MTEB measures Turkish, not Turkish morphology.

papers.title: TurkColBERT: A Benchmark of Dense and Late-Interaction Models for Turkish Information Retrieval
papers.approach: Two-stage adaptation: fine-tune English and multilingual encoders on Turkish NLI/STS, then convert them into ColBERT-style late-interaction retrievers with PyLate trained on MS MARCO-TR. Evaluates 10 models over five Turkish BEIR ports (SciFact-TR, ArguAna-TR, FiQA-TR, SciDocs-TR, NFCorpus-TR), and compares PLAID vs MUVERA(+rerank) indexing.
papers.key_results: Reported: colbert-hash-nano-tr (1.0M params) is ~600x smaller than turkish-e5-large (600M) while preserving >71% of its average mAP; ColmmBERT-base-TR gains up to +13.8% mAP on domain-specific tasks; MUVERA+Rerank gives +1.7% relative mAP over PLAID and is 3.33x faster; ColmmBERT-base-TR query time 0.54 ms under MUVERA. Per-dataset mAP extracted from the HTML for ColmmBERT-base-TR: SciFact-TR 56.8, ArguAna-TR 17.3, FiQA-TR 19.5, SciDocs-TR 6.8, NFCorpus-TR 11.5 — these came from an automated table read and should be re-checked against the PDF before citing.
papers.why_relevant: The single most directly relevant paper: it is the only Turkish work that systematically pits late interaction against single-vector dense encoders, and it motivates late interaction explicitly by Turkish agglutination and the single-vector 'information bottleneck'. Important caveat for the report: the paper *motivates* with morphology but (as far as I could read) does not run a morphology-specific error analysis, tokenization/fertility study, or suffix-level probe. So it is evidence that late interaction wins on Turkish BEIR, not evidence that it preserves suffix signal.

papers.title: TurkEmbed4Retrieval: Turkish Embedding Model for Retrieval Task
papers.approach: Retrieval-specialized variant of TurkEmbed: GTE-multilingual-base backbone with early layers frozen and deeper layers fine-tuned on MS MARCO-TR, using Matryoshka representation learning plus a tailored multiple-negatives ranking loss.
papers.key_results: Claims to outperform 'Turkish colBERT' by 19.26% on key retrieval metrics for SciFact-TR (snippet-level; metric name not confirmed).
papers.why_relevant: Directly comparable recipe to what the project plans (contrastive fine-tune a multilingual dual-encoder for Turkish retrieval), and it contradicts TurkColBERT's late-interaction-wins narrative on at least one dataset — worth flagging as an unresolved disagreement in the literature.

papers.title: NevIR: Negation in Neural Information Retrieval
papers.approach: Minimal-pair retrieval benchmark: the model must rank two documents that differ *only* by negation, scored with pairwise accuracy rather than nDCG. Evaluates sparse, bi-encoder, late-interaction, and cross-encoder architectures, plus continued fine-tuning on negation-containing contrastive data.
papers.key_results: Reported ordering by architecture: cross-encoders best, then late-interaction, then bi-encoders and sparse. Most IR models — including SOTA ones — perform the same as or worse than random ranking. Fine-tuning on negation data helps but a large human-machine gap remains; scale helps only marginally. I saw these as claims in the abstract, not as a numeric table.
papers.why_relevant: This is the methodological template for the project's morphological eval set: a single-feature minimal pair, pairwise accuracy, and a random baseline. It is also the strongest counter-evidence to the hope that late interaction automatically preserves fine-grained polarity signal — ColBERT-style models beat bi-encoders here but still sit around/below random. Turkish negation is a suffix (-me/-ma), so NevIR is almost literally the English analogue of the project's morph_counterfactual negatives.

papers.title: Reproducing NevIR: Negation in Neural Information Retrieval
papers.approach: Reproduction and extension of NevIR to more recent IR models, including listwise LLM re-rankers.
