papers.key_results: Snippet-level: cross-encoders perform best (slightly above random) while bi-encoder, sparse, and late-interaction architectures perform worse than random; listwise LLM re-rankers outperform others but still fall short of human performance.
papers.why_relevant: Confirms the NevIR result holds for newer models, and gives the sharper claim that late-interaction models specifically land *below random* on polarity minimal pairs — directly relevant to the project's 'does ColBERT keep the suffix?' question.

papers.title: Optimized Text Embedding Models and Benchmarks for Amharic Passage Retrieval
papers.approach: Trains Amharic-specific dense retrievers on Amharic BERT/RoBERTa backbones, plus a ColBERT late-interaction variant, and benchmarks against multilingual baselines. Frames the problem as data scarcity plus suboptimal tokenization for a morphologically complex language.
papers.key_results: RoBERTa-Base-Amharic-Embed (110M) achieves +17.6% relative MRR@10 and +9.86% Recall@10 over the strongest multilingual baseline Arctic Embed 2.0 (568M). RoBERTa-Medium-Amharic-Embed (42M) stays competitive at >13x smaller. The ColBERT late-interaction model attains the highest MRR@10 overall at 0.843.
papers.why_relevant: The closest non-Turkish analogue: a small language-specific encoder beating a much larger multilingual one on a morphologically rich language, with late interaction on top. Strong external support for the project's 'small dedicated morphological channel + LoRA' bet, and useful for the parameter-efficiency argument.

papers.title: The Multilingual Curse at the Retrieval Layer: Evidence from Amharic
papers.approach: Diagnostic study across four retrieval paradigms (dense, late interaction, learned sparse, cross-encoder) on a 68K query-passage Amharic benchmark, comparing zero-shot multilingual retrievers, fine-tuned multilingual retrievers, and monolingual models.
papers.key_results: Best zero-shot multilingual retriever trails the best monolingual Amharic model by ~23% relative MRR@10 (0.653 vs 0.803). Amharic-specific fine-tuning yields 32–60% relative gains over zero-shot, yet fine-tuned multilingual models still stay below monolingual ones despite ~2.5x more parameters. Attributes part of the gap to multilingual tokenizers over-segmenting the language's affixation and script.
papers.why_relevant: The clearest published statement that multilingual dense retrievers structurally under-serve morphologically complex languages and that fine-tuning alone does not close the gap — i.e., an argument for changing the *tokenization/representation*, not just the training data. Directly supports adding a dedicated morphological channel rather than only LoRA-tuning mE5/BGE-M3.

papers.title: Adapting Multilingual Embedding Models to Turkish via Cross-Lingual Tokenizer Surgery and Offline Distillation
papers.approach: Three stages: (1) build a 128K Turkish-optimized vocabulary by pruning redundant tokens and merging multilingual selections; (2) clone the teacher, keep transformer weights, remap the embedding matrix by mean-composition averaging of the old subword pieces; (3) offline distillation against precomputed teacher embeddings with cosine loss. Teacher EmbeddingGemma-300M -> student 200M / 128K vocab / 8K context, trained on balanced 40-language Wikipedia (~580K examples).
papers.key_results: STSbTR 77.55 Pearson / 77.45 Spearman (6th of 21 models), beating the teacher's 73.84 / 72.92. TR-MTEB 26-task average 63.9 (7th of 26) vs teacher 65.2. Relative to the teacher: +4.6% STS, +7.3% NLI. Training cost quoted at $5–$20 and ~4 GPU hours. The authors attribute gains to reduced fragmentation of agglutinative word forms into non-morphemic subwords.
papers.why_relevant: A cheap, concrete recipe for injecting Turkish morphological structure into an existing multilingual embedder without full retraining — an alternative or complement to LoRA contrastive fine-tuning. Note the honest signal: STS/NLI improved but the TR-MTEB average slightly *dropped* versus the teacher, so tokenizer surgery is not a free win for retrieval.

papers.title: Morpheus: A Morphology-Aware Neural Tokenizer and Word Embedder for Turkish
papers.approach: A lossless, morpheme-boundary-respecting neural tokenizer that simultaneously produces word embeddings, using a differentiable Poisson-binomial dynamic program over character-level boundary probabilities; encode-decode is exactly reversible.
papers.key_results: Bits-per-character 1.425 (lowest among reversible tokenizers compared); MorphScore macro-F1 0.61 vs ~0.32 for subword tokenizers; ~19% less memory than 64K-vocab subword models. Embedding side: root-family MAP 0.85 and same-root verification ROC-AUC 1.00, beating BGE-M3 and BERTurk on those lexical tasks — while contextual encoders remain better on context-dependent tasks such as NER and inflection probing.
papers.why_relevant: The most direct published candidate/blueprint for a *morphological channel encoder*: it is explicitly a lightweight, morphology-aligned Turkish embedder, and it reports the exact kind of diagnostic (root-family MAP, same-root verification) the project should adopt alongside its suffix probe. The reported weakness on inflection probing is itself a finding: root identity is easy, inflection is not.

papers.title: HeceTokenizer: A Syllable-Based Tokenization Approach for Turkish Retrieval
papers.approach: Exploits Turkish phonotactics to define a closed vocabulary of ~8,000 syllable types (no OOV), then trains a very small BERT (1.5M params) with masked LM and uses it for chunk-based retrieval.
papers.key_results: 50.3% Recall@5 on the TQuAD retrieval benchmark with chunk-based retrieval, versus 46.92% for a morphology-driven baseline that the paper says is ~200x larger.
papers.why_relevant: Evidence that a sub-2M-parameter Turkish-specific sublexical encoder can be retrieval-competitive — the strongest existence proof that a cheap morphological channel is viable. Also a reminder that syllable segmentation is a competitive alternative to morpheme segmentation for Turkish.

papers.title: Pooling and Semantic Shift: The Fundamental Challenges in Long Text Embedding and Retrieval
papers.approach: Formal analysis of pooling in single-vector text embedding, with two theorems plus empirical validation on ArXiv and a literary corpus using bge-large.
papers.key_results: Theorem 1 (semantic dilution): the discrepancy between a pooled text embedding and its constituent sentences strictly increases with semantic diversity. Theorem 2 (pooling-induced collapse): contextual aggregation strictly reduces Mean Pairwise Distance of the vector space, with severity monotonically increasing in pooling scale k; cosine collapse accelerated by norm decay. Empirically, with k=10 sentence groups, Spearman rho = 0.8838 and Kendall tau = 0.7074 (p << 1e-100) between semantic diversity and text-sentence discrepancy; random concatenation gave ~3x larger MPD drops than simple repetition.
papers.why_relevant: This is the best formal backing I found for the project's hypothesis that mean pooling washes out a single suffix in a long passage: it proves that a locally distinctive signal is provably diluted as pooling scale grows. Caveat to state honestly in the report — the theory is about *sentence-level* semantic diversity, not about a one-morpheme edit, so it is supporting theory by analogy, not direct evidence about suffixes. A related paper, 'Lost in a Single Vector: Improving Long-Document Retrieval with Chunk Evidence Aggregation' (arXiv:2606.18781), makes the same argument empirically for short evidence spans in long documents.

papers.title: LINSPECTOR: Multilingual Probing Tasks for Word Representations
papers.approach: A suite of morpho-syntactic and morpho-semantic probing tasks (POS, case marking, gender, tense, number, mood/polarity-style features), plus pseudo-word, comparative, and counting tasks, applied to word representations across typologically diverse languages, with correlation analysis against downstream task performance.
papers.key_results: Reported that Case, POS, Person, Tense, and TagCount probes correlate relatively highly with downstream performance in Finnish, Turkish, German, and Russian, and that several probes have significantly high positive correlation to downstream tasks specifically for morphologically rich languages.
papers.why_relevant: Gives an off-the-shelf, Turkish-supported probing methodology and task inventory for the morphological channel encoder — and empirical justification that morphological probe scores actually predict downstream quality for Turkish, which is exactly the assumption the project's Section C suffix probe and Section E selection matrix rely on.

papers.title: When Hard Negatives Hurt: Bridging the Generative-Discriminative Gap in Hard Negative Synthesis for Retrieval
papers.approach: Diagnoses why LLM-synthesized hard negatives degrade contrastive retrieval training, then proposes CausalNeg: chain-of-thought-guided counterfactual perturbation (decompose why a document satisfies a query into explicit information requirements, then violate one requirement at a time) plus Query-View Entropy Maximization to suppress source-identity shortcuts.
papers.key_results: Two failure modes: discriminative-agnostic generation (24% of generated negatives form 'pure clusters' isolated from other document types) and source-dependent shortcuts (models learn to discriminate by generation origin rather than relevance). Vanilla generation yields near-zero retrieval (nDCG@10 0.00–6.82) and naive mixing degrades 3 of 4 datasets. CausalNeg: mMARCO-zh 71.78 nDCG@10 (+1.90 over mining-only), HotpotQA 57.23 (+1.35), NQ 78.17 (+1.02), TriviaQA 59.02 (+2.27); avg +1.90 over mined-only and +3.50 over unregularized mixing.
papers.why_relevant: Critical warning for the team's next step (LLM-synthesizing a much larger typed-hard-negative set). It says: (a) do not naively mix LLM-generated negatives with mined ones, (b) generate by *surgically violating one stated requirement* — which is precisely the typed-negative schema the team already uses (morph_counterfactual, same_feature_wrong_content, partial_trap, state_variant), and (c) LLM-written negatives leak stylistic fingerprints that the encoder will shortcut on, so add a regularizer or match the surface distribution of golds.

techniques.name: Minimal-pair pairwise accuracy instead of nDCG for the morphology eval
techniques.description: Score the morphological eval set the NevIR way: present exactly two candidates that differ by one morpheme and measure whether the model ranks the correct one higher (pairwise accuracy), with an explicit 50% random baseline. This is far more sensitive than nDCG@10 over ~11 candidates, where a model can look fine by getting the topic right.
techniques.applicability: The existing 50-query x ~11-candidate set already contains typed single-feature negatives; derive a paired view (gold vs each morph_counterfactual) and report per-type pairwise accuracy alongside nDCG@10. Reporting 'below random' cases is a headline-grade finding, exactly as NevIR did for English.
techniques.evidence: NevIR (Weller et al., EACL 2024) reports most IR models perform at or below random ranking on negation minimal pairs; the SIGIR 2025 reproduction reports late-interaction, bi-encoder and sparse models all below random.

techniques.name: Late-interaction (ColBERT/MaxSim) as the morphological channel
techniques.description: Keep per-token vectors and score with MaxSim instead of collapsing to a single pooled vector, so a suffix-bearing token can match its counterpart directly rather than being averaged away.
techniques.applicability: Strong candidate architecture for the morph channel encoder, and the Turkish tooling exists (PyLate, MS MARCO-TR, MUVERA/PLAID indexing). But treat 'late interaction preserves suffix signal' as a hypothesis to test, not a given — the project is well positioned to be the first to actually measure it in Turkish.
techniques.evidence: TurkColBERT (arXiv:2511.16528) reports late-interaction models 3-5x smaller outperforming dense encoders on Turkish BEIR, and colbert-hash-nano-tr (1.0M) retaining >71% of turkish-e5-large's (600M) average mAP. Counter-evidence: NevIR and its SIGIR 2025 reproduction find late-interaction models at or below random on negation minimal pairs, so MaxSim is not automatically a fine-grained-polarity fix.

techniques.name: Morphology-aligned tokenization / vocabulary surgery on a multilingual backbone
techniques.description: Replace or augment the backbone's subword vocabulary with a Turkish-optimized one (morpheme-aligned, syllable-based, or pruned-and-merged), remapping old embeddings by mean composition, then distill offline against the original teacher's embeddings with cosine loss.
techniques.applicability: A cheap pre-step before LoRA contrastive fine-tuning: it reduces the fragmentation of agglutinative surface forms into non-morphemic pieces, which is the mechanistic story behind poor morphological sensitivity. Budget-wise it is trivial (~4 GPU hours in the cited work).
techniques.evidence: Bayram, Diri & Yıldırım (arXiv:2605.29992): 128K Turkish vocab + offline distillation from EmbeddingGemma-300M gives STSbTR 77.55/77.45 vs teacher 73.84/72.92 (+4.6% STS, +7.3% NLI) — but TR-MTEB average slipped to 63.9 vs teacher 65.2, so verify on retrieval specifically. Morpheus (arXiv:2606.18717) reports MorphScore macro-F1 0.61 vs ~0.32 for subword tokenizers.

techniques.name: Root-family MAP and same-root verification as morph-channel diagnostics
techniques.description: Two cheap intrinsic metrics: (a) given a word, retrieve other surface forms sharing its root and score MAP over the root family; (b) binary same-root/different-root verification scored by ROC-AUC. Complements a suffix-difference probe by testing the orthogonal axis (invariance to inflection vs sensitivity to inflection).
techniques.applicability: Add to notebook Section C. The morphological channel must do both: cluster forms of the same root together AND separate minimal suffix pairs. Measuring only one axis lets a degenerate encoder look good — a pure stemmer aces root-family MAP and fails every suffix counterfactual.
techniques.evidence: Morpheus (arXiv:2606.18717) reports root-family MAP 0.85 and same-root verification ROC-AUC 1.00, exceeding BGE-M3 and BERTurk, while noting contextual encoders still beat it on inflection probing.

techniques.name: Requirement-violating counterfactual generation for LLM-synthesized negatives (CausalNeg style)
techniques.description: Instead of asking an LLM for 'a similar but wrong passage', first make it enumerate the explicit information requirements that make the gold passage answer the query, then generate a negative that violates exactly one requirement. Pair with a regularizer (e.g. entropy maximization over the query-view similarity distribution) so the encoder cannot shortcut on 'this text was LLM-written'.
techniques.applicability: This is the direct recipe for scaling the 50-query set to thousands. The project's existing typed taxonomy (morph_counterfactual, same_feature_wrong_content, partial_trap, state_variant) already IS a requirement-violation taxonomy — formalize the prompt around it. Critically: do not naively mix synthesized negatives into the mined-negative pool for the LoRA training run.
techniques.evidence: arXiv:2606.01304 reports vanilla LLM generation yields nDCG@10 of 0.00-6.82, naive mixing degrades 3 of 4 datasets, 24% of generated negatives form isolated 'pure clusters'; CausalNeg recovers +1.90 avg nDCG@10 over mining-only and +3.50 over unregularized mixing.

techniques.name: Pooling alternatives to counter suffix dilution in long passages
techniques.description: Replace plain mean pooling with a pooling scheme that preserves local salient signal: anchor-token-aware weighted pooling, landmark-token pooling over chunks, last-token pooling, or chunk-level evidence aggregation with a max/soft-max over chunk scores.
techniques.applicability: Cheap ablation for the semantic encoder: hold the backbone fixed and swap pooling, then re-run the morphological eval as a function of passage length. If the suffix effect is a pooling artifact rather than a representation artifact, this is where it shows up — and it is a much smaller intervention than a second encoder.
techniques.evidence: Gao et al. (arXiv:2603.21437) prove pooling strictly increases pooled-vs-constituent discrepancy with semantic diversity and strictly reduces mean pairwise distance, with severity increasing in pooling scale k (empirical rho=0.8838, tau=0.7074). 'Lost in a Single Vector' (arXiv:2606.18781) makes the same point for short evidence spans in long documents.

techniques.name: Passage-length-stratified morphological evaluation
techniques.description: Construct the synthesized eval set so the same suffix contrast appears embedded in short (1 sentence), medium, and long (multi-paragraph) passages, and report morphological accuracy as a curve over passage length rather than a single number.
techniques.applicability: This is the experiment that would actually answer the team's own open question ('does mean pooling wash out a single suffix in a long passage?'). I found no paper that runs it for morphology in any language — it is a genuinely open, publishable slot, and it costs only a controlled generation template.
techniques.evidence: Motivated by the pooling-dilution theorems (arXiv:2603.21437) and the localized-evidence argument (arXiv:2606.18781); no direct morphological study found.

techniques.name: Classical stemming / prefix-truncation sparse baselines and hybrid fusion
techniques.description: Index with a Turkish stemmer, a lemmatizer, and naive fixed-prefix truncation (notably first-5 characters), run BM25 over each, and fuse with the dense scores (RRF or weighted). Also try character n-gram indexing as a conflation alternative.
techniques.applicability: A near-free, high-credibility baseline row for the selection matrix and for the final paper. Turkish agglutination fragments lexical evidence across surface forms, so sparse-dense hybrids are the standard remedy; and if F5-truncated BM25 matches a fine-tuned dense encoder on the morphological set, that is a result worth reporting rather than hiding.
techniques.evidence: Can & Kocberber (JASIST 2008): on a 408,305-document / 72-query Turkish collection, simple truncation, statistics-based truncation, and lemmatizer-based stemming give broadly similar effectiveness, with prefix length 5 effective. Ekmekçioğlu et al. (Information Research, 1996) for n-gram conflation. MIRACL reports mDPR below BM25 yet still additive in hybrids.

techniques.name: Morphological probing classifiers over frozen representations (LINSPECTOR style)
techniques.description: Train small linear/MLP probes on frozen encoder outputs to predict morphological features (case, tense, person, number, polarity, possession, tag count) from Turkish annotated data, and report per-feature accuracy as an encoder-selection signal.
techniques.applicability: A more diagnostic alternative to the current 50-triplet pilot probe: it tells you *which* morphological features an encoder encodes, so the morphological channel can be targeted at the ones the semantic encoder loses. LINSPECTOR ships Turkish tasks and data.
techniques.evidence: Şahin et al., Computational Linguistics 46(2) 2020: Case, POS, Person, Tense and TagCount probes correlate relatively strongly with downstream performance in Turkish, Finnish, German and Russian.

techniques.name: Small language-specific encoder over large multilingual, for the morph channel
techniques.description: Train or adapt a small Turkish-only sublexical/morphological encoder rather than relying on a large multilingual model to carry the morphological signal, and keep the multilingual model for the semantic channel.
techniques.applicability: Validates the two-encoder architecture at the parameter budget the project cares about: the morph channel can plausibly be 1-42M parameters and still contribute real signal, keeping LoRA fine-tuning cheap.
techniques.evidence: Amharic (Findings ACL 2025): 110M monolingual beats 568M Arctic Embed 2.0 by +17.6% relative MRR@10; 42M variant stays competitive at 13x smaller. 'The Multilingual Curse' (arXiv:2605.24556): best zero-shot multilingual trails best monolingual by ~23% relative MRR@10 (0.653 vs 0.803) and fine-tuned multilingual models still lose despite 2.5x more parameters. HeceTokenizer (arXiv:2604.10665): 1.5M-param syllable BERT reaches 50.3% Recall@5 on TQuAD.

techniques.name: Report retrieval efficiency and index footprint alongside quality
techniques.description: Log query latency and index size per candidate model and indexing scheme (PLAID vs MUVERA+rerank for late interaction; flat vs quantized for single-vector), not just nDCG.
techniques.applicability: Feeds Section D/E of the selection notebook directly and makes the 'small morphological channel' argument concrete: a second encoder is only defensible if the combined system stays cheap.
techniques.evidence: TurkColBERT (arXiv:2511.16528) reports MUVERA+Rerank at +1.7% relative mAP and 3.33x faster than PLAID, with ColmmBERT-base-TR at 0.54 ms query time.

techniques.name: Treat translated Turkish-BEIR ports as a soft benchmark, and add a native-Turkish morphological set
techniques.description: Because scifact-tr / nfcorpus-tr / arguana-tr / fiqa-tr are machine- or human-translated from English, their surface morphology is likely simpler and more regular than native Turkish, and the query-document lexical overlap is translationese-inflated. Keep them for comparability but do not let them carry the morphological claim.
techniques.applicability: Justifies the project's held-out native morphological eval set as the primary evidence and the Turkish-BEIR runs as the secondary comparability layer — exactly the split the notebooks already use. Say this explicitly in the paper's limitations.
techniques.evidence: TurkColBERT itself lists reliance on 'moderately sized datasets (<=50K documents) and translated benchmarks' as a limitation; TR-MTEB is described as incorporating both native and translated resources.

gaps: No published minimal-pair morphological RETRIEVAL benchmark exists for Turkish, as far as I could find. NevIR is English-only and negation-only. The team's 50-query typed-negative set appears to be genuinely novel as an artifact — this is the strongest publishable angle I saw.

TurkColBERT motivates late interaction with Turkish agglutination but (in what I could read) never runs a morphology-specific analysis: no fertility/tokenization study, no suffix-level probe, no per-morphological-phenomenon breakdown. So the claim 'late interaction preserves suffix signal in Turkish' is currently UNTESTED — asserted by architecture intuition, not measured.

Direct evidence that mean pooling specifically washes out a single suffix in a long passage does not exist that I could find. What exists is (a) formal proof that pooling dilutes locally distinctive signal as pooling scale grows (arXiv:2603.21437) and (b) empirical work on short evidence spans in long documents (arXiv:2606.18781). The morphology-specific version is an open experiment — run the eval stratified by passage length.

The two most relevant Turkish papers disagree and nobody has reconciled them: TurkColBERT claims late-interaction models beat dense encoders on Turkish BEIR, while TurkEmbed4Retrieval claims to beat 'Turkish colBERT' by 19.26% on SciFact-TR. Different training data, different metrics (mAP vs unspecified), possibly different ColBERT checkpoints. Worth a sentence acknowledging the conflict rather than citing whichever supports the project.

I found no Turkish-specific study of tokenizer fertility -> retrieval quality. The fertility literature for Turkish (arXiv:2502.07057, TALLIP 2023 'Impact of Tokenization on Language Models', arXiv:2508.14292 'Tokens with Meaning') evaluates NER/POS/QA/sentiment, not nDCG. The one retrieval-adjacent tokenizer paper (arXiv:2605.29992) shows tokenizer surgery helping STS/NLI while slightly HURTING the TR-MTEB average — an unexplained and important negative result.

Mizan (newmindai) appears to be a leaderboard with no accompanying paper I could locate — so its scores are un-peer-reviewed and its snapshot date is not documented anywhere I found. Keep it as a cited column, never averaged with TR-MTEB, exactly as the project's CLAUDE.md already says.

No work I found evaluates whether specific Turkish morphological categories differ in retrieval difficulty (negation -me/-ma vs case vs tense vs evidentiality vs causative). The typed-negative taxonomy in the team's eval set could produce the first such breakdown.

I could not verify the classical Can & Kocberber (2008) result cleanly: one search snippet says truncation and lemmatization are comparable, another says the lemmatizer is significantly better. Both PDF fetch attempts failed (Semantic Scholar returned an empty body). Someone should pull the actual JASIST paper or the Bilkent repository copy before citing a specific claim.

Multilingual retriever weaknesses on morphology are mostly asserted through the low-resource lens (data scarcity + tokenization), not isolated experimentally. I found no ablation that holds training data fixed and varies only the tokenizer's morphological alignment for a retrieval objective. That controlled experiment appears to be missing across all languages.

Nothing found on how to COMBINE a semantic and a morphological channel at scoring time for retrieval (score fusion vs concatenated embedding vs gated). The dual-encoder-with-a-morph-channel design does not seem to have a published Turkish precedent to copy.
confidence: Medium-high on the overall landscape; mixed at the level of individual numbers. Fully verified by reading (fetched_fulltext): TurkColBERT, The Multilingual Curse (Amharic), tokenizer-surgery/distillation for Turkish, Pooling and Semantic Shift, CausalNeg. Abstract-level only (saw_abstract): TR-MTEB, NevIR, Amharic Findings-ACL-2025, Morpheus, HeceTokenizer. Snippet-only and therefore weakest: the four classical Turkish IR papers, TurkEmbed4Retrieval, Reproducing NevIR, LINSPECTOR. Specific cautions: (1) the TurkColBERT per-dataset mAP figures (SciFact-TR 56.8, ArguAna-TR 17.3, FiQA-TR 19.5, SciDocs-TR 6.8, NFCorpus-TR 11.5) came from an automated read of the HTML table and the same read returned implausible dataset statistics elsewhere (e.g. it reported SciFact-TR with 1,110 queries / 5,180 docs, which looks like swapped or garbled fields) — re-check against the PDF before publishing any of those numbers. (2) I could not retrieve per-model retrieval scores from TR-MTEB; both PDF fetches returned undecoded binary. (3) Author lists for CausalNeg and for two of the classical Turkish papers are incomplete — I saw only partial attributions. (4) Several arXiv IDs here are 2026-dated preprints (2603.*, 2604.*, 2605.*, 2606.*) that may not be peer-reviewed; weight them accordingly. (5) Anything I marked search_snippet_only reflects a search-engine summary, not text I read on the source page, and the Can & Kocberber stemming conclusion in particular is internally contradictory across snippets. No number in this report was inferred or reconstructed — where I did not see it, the field is null.

topic: tr-morph-nlp — How Turkish morphology has been handled in NLP models: analyzers/disambiguators, treebanks, Turkish LMs, tokenizer/vocabulary quality, and morphological segmentation. Focus: what concretely improved a model's grasp of Turkish suffix semantics, and what did not.
confidence: Medium-high on the modern tokenizer/LM literature (2022-2026), where I fetched and read primary pages; medium on the classical analyzer/treebank layer (Oflazer, Zemberek, Sak, Yuret & Türe, BOUN/IMST), where I only saw search snippets and secondary citations — treat those years, venues and accuracy numbers as needing a one-click verification before they go in a report. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: four of the most directly on-topic items (Morpheus 2606.18717, HeceTokenizer 2604.10665, Optimal Turkish Subword Strategies 2602.06942, Tokenizer Surgery 2605.29992) are 2026 arXiv preprints, several single-author and apparently unrefereed; their numbers are self-reported and I read them from the paper's own abstract/HTML, not from independent replication. I did NOT successfully read the MorphScore-70 full text (the PDF fetch returned no correlation statistics), so its headline negative finding is search-snippet-level only and should be verified directly at arXiv:2507.06378 / OpenReview XYRri1s6pP before being quoted. I did not find any paper that does exactly what your team is doing (a separate morphological channel encoder fused with a semantic encoder, LoRA contrastive, for Turkish retrieval) — that appears to be genuinely unoccupied ground.

papers.title: Two-level Description of Turkish Morphology
papers.approach: Finite-state two-level (Koskenniemi-style) morphotactics + morphophonemic rules for Turkish. Repeatedly cited across the newer literature as the first practical and most influential Turkish morphological analyzer, and the ancestor of essentially every rule-based Turkish analyzer since.
papers.why_relevant: This is the origin of the root+suffix-chain representation (e.g. ev+Noun+A3pl+P1pl+Abl) that every downstream Turkish morphology resource, including UD feature conversion and the tag inventories used in modern probes, inherits. If you want typed suffix labels for your morphological channel, this is the schema lineage.

papers.title: A Freely Available Morphological Analyzer for Turkish (TRmorph)
papers.approach: Two-level FST analyzer implemented entirely with free tools (SFST): a lexicon, an FSA over morphotactics, and a set of two-level phonological rules. Distributed under a permissive license; a trmorph2 branch exists on GitHub (coltekin/TRmorph). Evaluated on two large corpora.
papers.why_relevant: The most practical free, inspectable, non-Java analyzer for generating gold suffix segmentations and morphological feature tags at scale. Directly usable to auto-label the morpheme boundaries and feature types (case, tense, negation, possessive) you need for typed hard negatives, without an LLM in the loop.

papers.title: Zemberek, an open source NLP framework for Turkic languages
papers.approach: Open-source Java framework providing morphological analysis, morphological ambiguity resolution (disambiguation) and word generation. The generation direction is the underused part: you can synthesize a surface form from root + feature bundle.
papers.why_relevant: Zemberek's *generation* API is the cleanest way to build morph_counterfactual negatives programmatically and deterministically — take the gold positive, flip exactly one feature (Neg, Abl->Dat, Past->Aor), regenerate the surface form. That gives you guaranteed single-suffix minimal pairs rather than LLM-guessed ones, and it's how you can validate the LLM-synthesized set you're about to build.

papers.title: Turkish Language Resources: Morphological Parser, Morphological Disambiguator and Web Corpus / Resources for Turkish morphological processing
papers.venue: GoTAL 2008; extended in Language Resources and Evaluation (2011)
papers.approach: Stochastic FST-based morphological parser plus an averaged-perceptron reranker over the n-best list of candidate morphological parses for disambiguation. Trained on the semi-automatically disambiguated ~1M-token corpus of Yuret & Türe (2006), with a manually annotated ~20K-token test set built to make Turkish disambiguation systems comparable.
papers.key_results: Search snippets reported perceptron disambiguation accuracy figures of 96.80% and 97.81% on the test set. I did NOT read these off the paper itself — verify before citing.
papers.why_relevant: This is the disambiguator whose output was used to bootstrap the morphological features in the BOUN treebank, so its error modes propagate into Turkish UD morphology. Also the standard reference for 'how good is automatic Turkish morphological tagging' — roughly 97%, which is good enough to auto-label your eval set but not good enough to skip human QC (which your reviewer_C pass already reflects).

papers.title: Resources for Turkish Dependency Parsing: Introducing the BOUN Treebank and the BoAT Annotation Tool
papers.approach: Manually annotated UD treebank. Morphological features and UPOS are first produced automatically by the Sak et al. parser and converted to UD, then manually corrected. A follow-up (arXiv:2207.11782) re-annotates BOUN to handle null morphemes, heavy agglutination, and syncretic morphemes such as the copula and -ki.
papers.why_relevant: BOUN plus UD_Turkish-IMST (a semi-automatic conversion of IMST, itself a re-annotation of the METU-Sabancı treebank; ~5,635 sentences from news and novels shared across all three) are your only sizeable gold sources of Turkish morphological feature annotations in a standard schema. The published re-annotation notes are effectively a list of the hard cases (-ki, copula, syncretism, null morphemes) your eval set should deliberately include as partial_trap items.

papers.title: Building Morphological Chains for Agglutinative Languages
papers.approach: Log-linear MorphoChains model extended so the candidate space is expanded recursively rather than binary-split, so a word can be segmented into an arbitrarily long suffix chain — the right inductive bias for agglutinative Turkish. Related: Üstün & Can, 'Unsupervised Morphological Segmentation Using Neural Word Embeddings' (SLSP 2016), which adds distributional/semantic features to segmentation.
papers.key_results: Reported improvement over state of the art for Turkish by 12%, to F-measure 72%; English improved 3% to F-measure 74%. Reported to beat MorphoChains and other well-known unsupervised segmenters. Numbers from search snippet, not read off the paper.
papers.why_relevant: Two takeaways for your morph encoder: (a) binary segmentation assumptions built into most Morfessor-style baselines are wrong for Turkish, you need recursive chains; (b) adding *semantic* (embedding) features improved segmentation — i.e. the morphology and semantics channels helped each other, which is an argument for jointly training your two encoders rather than freezing the morph channel.

papers.title: Impact of Tokenization on Language Models: An Analysis for Turkish
papers.approach: Trained five tokenizers spanning character -> word granularity, explicitly including a Morphological-level tokenizer, then pretrained matched medium-size RoBERTa models on the Turkish split of OSCAR and evaluated downstream with statistical testing.
papers.key_results: Morphological-level tokenizer gives 'challenging' (competitive, not superior) performance versus the de facto BPE/WordPiece. BPE and WordPiece are roughly equivalent to each other. Word- and character-level tokenizers are drastically worse downstream. Increasing vocabulary size helps Morphological and Word-level tokenizers MORE than it helps BPE/WordPiece. Recommended vocabulary parameters at ~20% of total model parameters for de facto tokenizers, ~40% for the others.
papers.why_relevant: The most important calibration point in this whole survey: under matched pretraining, linguistically correct morphological tokenization did NOT beat BPE on downstream tasks. It only becomes competitive when you also grow the vocabulary. This is the strongest published reason not to bet the project on 'better segmentation alone' and instead to inject morphology as an auxiliary channel/objective, which is what your architecture already does.

papers.title: Tokens with Meaning: A Hybrid Tokenization Approach for Turkish
papers.authors_short: Bayram, Fincan, Gümüş, Karakaş, Diri, Yıldırım & Çelik
papers.approach: Three-part TurkishTokenizer: (1) dictionary-driven morphological segmentation — 22,231 root tokens mapped to 20,000 canonical IDs plus 72 affix IDs covering 177 surface forms; (2) phonological normalization mapping allomorphs (vowel harmony, consonant assimilation, lenition) onto shared IDs, so -den/-dan/-ten/-tan collapse to one identifier; (3) BPE fallback (12,696 tokens) for OOV. Longest-prefix matching, explicit rule-based decoding over 5 morphophonemic patterns.
papers.key_results: TR-MMLU: Turkish token percentage 90.29%, pure token percentage 85.80%, roundtrip exact-match reconstruction 99.48%. With randomly initialized models: STSb-TR Pearson 51.44% (vs Tabi 43.01, CosmosGPT2 43.09, Mursit 46.63); TR-MTEB overall average 39.57% (vs 34.92 / 35.65 / 35.92); TurBLiMP average pairwise accuracy 61.2% (vs 51.6 / 52.7 / 50.8). Cost: token density rises to 2.91 tokens/word vs 1.82 for BPE (~1.5x longer sequences). Classification results were mixed — Tabi won on specific benchmarks.
papers.why_relevant: The single most directly transferable idea for your morphological channel: allomorph normalization. Collapsing -den/-dan/-ten/-tan (and -ler/-lar, -di/-dı/-du/-dü) to one canonical affix ID means the ablative is one symbol regardless of vowel harmony — exactly the invariance a morph encoder needs, and exactly what surface BPE destroys. Note their gains are largest on STS and TR-MTEB (semantic similarity/retrieval), which is your task family, and weakest on classification.

papers.title: Optimal Turkish Subword Strategies at Scale: Systematic Evaluation of Data–Vocabulary–Morphology Interplay
papers.approach: Jointly sweeps vocabulary size and tokenizer-training-corpus size (up to ~80GB) across WordPiece, BPE, morphology-aware and character baselines under matched parameter budgets. Introduces a morphology-aware diagnostic suite: boundary-level micro/macro-F1 against gold morpheme boundaries, lemma boundary hit rate (does the stem/suffix cut survive), over-/under-segmentation indices, continuation rates, affix-type coverage. Evaluates on TrGLUE (CoLA, MNLI, MRPC, SST-2, STS-B), Turkish WikiNER, and BOUN (POS, dependency, morphological tagging).
papers.key_results: Character-level: 91.56 POS accuracy, 65.19 UAS, 57.15 LAS on BOUN, morphological micro-accuracy 96.19 (near-ceiling on several categories) but large gaps on STS-B and CoLA. Word-level collapses: ~60 POS, ~19 LAS, ~12 morphology F1; NER F1 saturating ~0.5 vs ~0.70 for character/subword. Morphology-aware subword tokenizers gave 'small but consistent' gains on POS and NER over WordPiece, tied to affix atomicity. Explicit negative: morphology-TAG injection increases sequence length and generally HARMS downstream performance.
papers.why_relevant: This is the cleanest published answer to your key question. What helps Turkish suffix grasp: character-level granularity (morphological fidelity near ceiling) and affix-atomic subword vocabularies with enough vocab budget. What does NOT help: word-level vocabularies, and — critically — injecting morphological tags into the input sequence. Practical consequence for your design: make the morphological channel a *character-level or affix-ID encoder* and fuse its output embedding, rather than concatenating morph tags into the semantic encoder's input text. Also: character models are strong on morphology but weak on STS, which is precisely why a two-channel architecture makes sense.

papers.title: Evaluating Morphological Alignment of Tokenizers in 70 Languages (MorphScore v2)
papers.approach: Expands MorphScore from 22 to 70 languages; measures the extent to which a tokenizer segments words along gold morpheme boundaries. Then correlates those alignment scores with downstream task performance for five pretrained LMs across seven tasks, with at least one task per language. Code at github.com/catherinearnett/morphscore.
papers.key_results: Headline negative finding (from search snippet, NOT verified in full text — my PDF fetch returned no correlation statistics): morphological alignment does not significantly correlate with model performance across tasks, and does not explain much variance, suggesting alignment alone does not capture the dimensions of tokenization quality that matter for model performance. No Turkish-specific number obtained.
papers.why_relevant: The mandatory counterweight to every 'our tokenizer aligns better with morphemes' paper in this list. Direct implication for your selection matrix: do NOT let a morpheme-alignment score stand in as a proxy for retrieval quality. Your morph probe and your held-out eval set must be scored on retrieval metrics, not on segmentation F1. Verify this paper's claim yourself before quoting the number, since my fetch failed.

papers.title: Evaluating Morphological Compositional Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.authors_short: Ismayilzada, Circi, Sälevä, Sirin, Köksal, Dhingra, Bosselut, Ataman & van der Plas
papers.approach: Treats morphemes as compositional primitives and builds a suite of generative and discriminative tasks probing morphological productivity (can the model apply a known suffix to a novel root?) and systematicity (is behaviour consistent across combinations?). Evaluates instruction-finetuned multilingual LLMs including GPT-4, Gemini, Aya-23, Qwen-2.5, with human baselines.
papers.key_results: LLMs struggle with morphological compositional generalization, particularly on novel word roots, with performance declining sharply as morphological complexity increases. Models identify individual morphological combinations better than chance but lack systematicity, leaving significant accuracy gaps versus humans. (No tokenizer-effect analysis surfaced in the abstract I read.)
papers.why_relevant: Two direct consequences for your plan to LLM-synthesize a larger eval set. (1) Design: novel/rare roots and high suffix-stack depth are where models actually break, so stratify your synthesized queries by suffix-chain length and root frequency — a set built only from frequent roots will look easy and won't discriminate. (2) Risk: the LLM generating your data has exactly the weakness you are testing for, so it will likely produce systematically wrong inflections on rare roots. Validate LLM-generated surface forms with a rule-based generator (Zemberek/TRmorph) rather than trusting the LLM.

papers.title: TurBLiMP: A Turkish Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs
papers.approach: 16,000 minimal pairs over 16 grammatical phenomena (1,000 each), targeting flexible word order and the role of morphology in subordination. Three-stage construction: linguists hand-write 10 seed pairs per phenomenon to fix guidelines; semi-automatic augmentation uses masked BERTurk to propose lexical substitutions which are manually verified, giving 100 validated pairs per phenomenon; then fully automatic augmentation with BERTurk substitutions plus a Turkish morphology pipeline to inflect the substituted words correctly, scaling to 1,000. Includes newly collected human acceptability judgments.
papers.key_results: Even cutting-edge LLMs still struggle with phenomena that are easy for humans, and show different sensitivities to word order and morphological complexity than humans do.
papers.why_relevant: This is the closest published template for exactly the scaling step you are about to take, and it argues against a pure LLM-synthesis pipeline. Their recipe — small hand-built linguist seed set, model-proposed lexical substitution, then a RULE-BASED morphological inflector to produce the surface forms, with human verification at the 100-per-type checkpoint — is directly portable to expanding your 50-query set. The morphology pipeline in the loop is what keeps the negatives well-typed. Also worth noting TurBLiMP is already used as an evaluation target by the Tokens with Meaning paper, so it can serve as a secondary check on your chosen encoders.

papers.title: Morpheus: A Morphology-Aware Neural Tokenizer and Word Embedder for Turkish
papers.approach: A differentiable Poisson-binomial dynamic program converts per-character boundary probabilities into soft morpheme memberships at training time and exact segments at inference. Lossless and fully reversible (decode returns the original word). Doubles as a word embedder.
papers.key_results: 1.425 bits-per-character (lowest among reversible tokenizers); ~19% less GPU memory than 64K-vocab subword tokenizers; MorphScore macro-F1 0.61, roughly double the ~0.32 of the subword family; root-family retrieval MAP 0.85; same-root verification ROC-AUC 1.00; beats BGE-M3 and BERTurk on these lexical tasks. Explicit limitation: on context- and inflection-dependent tasks (NER, case/number probing) contextual encoders remain superior, attributed to Morpheus's root-centric geometry.
papers.why_relevant: Two things. (1) The failure mode is the exact hazard for your project: a root-centric morphology-aware embedder wins at same-root/root-family retrieval but LOSES on case/number probing — i.e. it learns 'these share a root' and not 'these differ by ablative vs dative'. Your typed negatives (morph_counterfactual, state_variant) are precisely case/number-style discriminations, so a root-centric morph channel could actively hurt. Guard against this by checking your morph encoder can separate same-root-different-suffix pairs, not just cluster same-root ones. (2) Root-family MAP and same-root ROC-AUC are cheap, reusable intrinsic metrics for your Section C probe. Caveat: single-author 2026 preprint, ROC-AUC 1.00 is a suspiciously saturated number.

papers.title: HeceTokenizer: A Syllable-Based Tokenization Approach for Turkish Retrieval
papers.approach: Exploits Turkish's deterministic six-pattern syllable phonology to build a closed, OOV-free vocabulary of ~8,000 syllable types. Trains a BERT-tiny (1.5M params) from scratch on Turkish Wikipedia with MLM, combined with fine-grained chunk-based retrieval.
papers.key_results: TQuAD retrieval, Recall@5: 50.3% for HeceTokenizer vs 46.92% for a morphology-driven baseline that used a model reported as 200x larger. No negative results reported by the authors.
papers.why_relevant: Relevant as a cheap, deterministic alternative for the *morphological channel encoder* specifically — syllabification is rule-based, needs no lexicon, has zero OOV, and a 1.5M-param model is essentially free to run alongside your semantic encoder. Since Turkish suffixes are largely syllable-aligned, syllables approximate morpheme units without a morphological analyzer. Treat the headline comparison sceptically though: single-author preprint, single dataset (TQuAD), one metric, and the 200x-smaller framing invites a favourable baseline choice.

papers.title: Adapting Multilingual Embedding Models to Turkish via Cross-Lingual Tokenizer Surgery and Offline Distillation
papers.approach: Three stages. (1) Tokenizer surgery: build a 128K vocabulary by extracting Turkish tokens from the Cosmos Turkish Corpus and merging with frequency-selected multilingual tokens from a 40-language Wikipedia set. (2) Weight-preserving cloning: keep the transformer backbone, remap embeddings by mean-composition (average the teacher's embeddings of the old pieces to initialize each new token). (3) Offline distillation: train the student on precomputed teacher embeddings with cosine loss. Teacher EmbeddingGemma-300M (256K vocab); student ~205M params, 128K vocab, 8,192 context.
papers.key_results: STSbTR Pearson 77.55% vs teacher 73.84% (+3.71). TR-MTEB 26-task average 63.9% (7th of 26 models) vs teacher 65.2%. STS +4.6 and NLI +7.3 over teacher. ~98% of teacher performance with 33% fewer parameters. Training cost $5-20, ~4 hours on one A100. Stated limitations: degraded performance on non-target lower-resource languages; capacity loss from pruning 256K->128K; mean-composition vocabulary transfer ignores polysemy and context; linear pooling/projection may cap classification and clustering performance.
papers.why_relevant: The most operationally useful paper for your semantic encoder. It shows you can get a Turkish-native vocabulary onto a strong multilingual embedder for ~$20 and 4 GPU-hours without full retraining, and that this improves STS/NLI over the teacher while slightly LOSING on the TR-MTEB average — a nuance worth reproducing in your selection matrix rather than assuming vocabulary surgery is a free win. Note the honest negative: mean-composition initialization is a crude vocabulary transfer, which is a concrete thing your project could improve on.

papers.title: Information retrieval on Turkish texts
papers.authors_short: Can, Kocberber, Balcik, Kaynak, Ocalan & Vursavas
papers.approach: Large-scale classical IR study: 408,305 documents, 72 ad hoc queries. Compares simple fixed-length word truncation (3, 4, 5 characters), corpus-statistics-driven truncation, and an elaborate lemmatizer-based stemmer, crossed with different query-document matching functions.
papers.key_results: The three approaches — naive fixed-length truncation, statistics-based truncation, and the elaborate lemmatizer-based stemmer — provide SIMILAR retrieval effectiveness on Turkish.
papers.why_relevant: The oldest and most sobering 'what did NOT work' result in Turkish morphology-for-retrieval, and it predicts the modern MorphScore finding by 17 years: for retrieval specifically, sophisticated morphological analysis bought essentially nothing over chopping words at 5 characters. Two uses for you: (a) add a first-5-characters truncation + BM25 baseline to your eval — if your morphology-aware dual encoder cannot beat it on the held-out morph set, the morphology channel is not earning its keep; (b) this is the honest framing for your project's contribution — classical IR morphology helped with *lexical matching* (recall over inflected variants), whereas your set tests suffix *semantics* (ablative vs dative changes the answer), which truncation cannot possibly capture. That distinction is your motivation section.

techniques.name: Allomorph normalization to canonical affix IDs
techniques.description: Map every surface variant of a suffix onto a single identifier before or during encoding: -den/-dan/-ten/-tan -> ABL, -ler/-lar -> PLUR, -di/-dı/-du/-dü/-ti/-tı -> PAST. The Tokens with Meaning tokenizer does this explicitly with 72 affix IDs covering 177 surface forms, plus rules for vowel harmony, consonant assimilation and lenition, and still decodes losslessly (99.48% roundtrip exact match).
techniques.evidence: Tokens with Meaning (arXiv:2508.14292v3) — 90.29% Turkish token percentage, 85.80% pure tokens, and its biggest downstream gains are on STSb-TR (51.44 vs 43-47 for Turkish baselines) and TR-MTEB (39.57 vs 34.9-35.9), i.e. exactly the semantic-similarity/retrieval family.
techniques.applicability: This is the highest-value single idea for your morphological channel encoder. Feeding it canonical affix IDs rather than surface subwords gives the encoder vowel-harmony invariance for free, so 'evlerden' and 'kitaplardan' share the PLUR+ABL signature. It also makes your typed negatives cleanly constructible: a morph_counterfactual is literally one affix-ID substitution. Zemberek or TRmorph can produce the analyses; the affix ID table is the vocabulary of your morph channel.

techniques.name: Rule-based generation for building minimal-pair negatives (not LLM generation)
techniques.description: Instead of asking an LLM to write a wrong-suffix variant, take the gold analysis root+features, flip exactly one feature, and regenerate the surface form with a rule-based generator. Zemberek exposes word generation; TRmorph's FST is bidirectional. This guarantees the negative differs by exactly one morpheme and is phonologically well-formed.
techniques.evidence: TurBLiMP (EMNLP 2025) used exactly this shape at scale: linguist-written seeds -> BERTurk proposes lexical substitutions -> a Turkish morphology pipeline inflects them correctly -> 1,000 validated pairs per phenomenon. Separately, Ismayilzada et al. (NAACL 2025) show LLMs themselves fail at morphological productivity on novel roots, i.e. the generator has the defect being tested.
techniques.applicability: Directly changes your plan to LLM-synthesize a larger eval set. Use the LLM for the *semantic* content (plausible queries, plausible distractor passages) and a rule-based generator for the *morphological* mutation. Otherwise your morph_counterfactual negatives will contain silent inflection errors on exactly the rare-root cases that are supposed to be the hard ones, and your benchmark will measure LLM inflection noise rather than encoder morphology.

techniques.name: Character-level or syllable-level morphological channel (not tag injection)
techniques.description: Make the morphological encoder operate at character or syllable granularity rather than pushing morphological feature tags into the semantic encoder's input string. Turkish syllabification follows six deterministic patterns, giving a closed ~8K OOV-free vocabulary with no lexicon required.
techniques.evidence: Altinok (arXiv:2602.06942) reports character-level models reaching 96.19 morphological micro-accuracy and 91.56 POS on BOUN (near-ceiling on several morphological categories) while being weak on STS-B/CoLA — AND reports explicitly that morphology-TAG tokenization increases sequence length and generally harms downstream performance. HeceTokenizer (arXiv:2604.10665) gets 50.3 Recall@5 on TQuAD from a 1.5M-param syllable model.
techniques.applicability: Two design rules for your architecture. First, the strong morphology/weak semantics profile of character models is the direct empirical justification for your two-encoder split — the channels are complementary, so do not try to make one model do both. Second, and concretely: do NOT implement the morphological channel by prepending morph tags to the query text. Encode the character/syllable stream separately and fuse at the embedding level.

techniques.name: Cross-lingual tokenizer surgery + offline distillation
techniques.description: Replace a strong multilingual embedder's vocabulary with a Turkish-heavy one, initialize each new token embedding by mean-composing the teacher's embeddings of the pieces it replaces, keep the transformer backbone frozen-ish, then distill on precomputed teacher embeddings with cosine loss. Reduces Turkish fragmentation without pretraining from scratch.
techniques.evidence: Bayram, Diri & Yıldırım (arXiv:2605.29992): student ~205M params from EmbeddingGemma-300M teacher, STSbTR 77.55 vs teacher 73.84, NLI +7.3, ~98% of teacher performance with 33% fewer params, $5-20 and ~4 hours on one A100. But TR-MTEB average 63.9 vs teacher 65.2 — a slight net loss on the aggregate benchmark.
techniques.applicability: A realistic alternative or complement to LoRA fine-tuning for your semantic encoder, at a cost your project can actually afford. Also gives you a specific, publishable improvement target: their own stated weakness is that mean-composition vocabulary transfer ignores polysemy and context. And their mixed result (STS up, TR-MTEB average down) is a warning to score any vocabulary change on your own retrieval metric, not to assume it transfers.

techniques.name: Boundary-level diagnostics instead of fertility alone
techniques.description: Replace single-number fertility with a diagnostic panel: micro/macro-F1 against gold morpheme boundaries, lemma boundary hit rate (does the stem/suffix cut survive), over- and under-segmentation indices, continuation-subword rate, affix-type coverage, token purity, and Turkish-token percentage.
techniques.evidence: Altinok (arXiv:2602.06942) defines this suite. Tokens with Meaning reports Turkish token % (90.29) and pure token % (85.80) and notes token density rises to 2.91 tokens/word vs 1.82 for BPE. A search result on Turkish tokenization measurement claimed language-specific token percentage correlates with model performance more strongly than token purity does.
techniques.applicability: Concrete additions to your notebook Section C and Section D. Compute lemma boundary hit rate and affix-type coverage per candidate model — these tell you whether a candidate's tokenizer even *can* see the suffix your eval set mutates. If a model shreds -den into ['d','en'] across a token boundary shared with the stem, no amount of contrastive fine-tuning will teach it ablative semantics cheaply. Also track token density, since 1.5x sequence length is a real cost in your efficiency column.

techniques.name: Root-family retrieval MAP and same-root verification ROC-AUC as intrinsic probes
techniques.description: Two cheap intrinsic tests of an embedding space's morphological structure: (a) given an inflected form as query, retrieve all forms sharing its root (report MAP); (b) binary same-root/different-root verification over form pairs (report ROC-AUC).
techniques.evidence: Morpheus (arXiv:2606.18717) reports root-family MAP 0.85 and same-root ROC-AUC 1.00, beating BGE-M3 and BERTurk — while explicitly conceding it loses to contextual encoders on case/number probing.
techniques.applicability: Add these alongside your existing 50-triplet suffix probe, but read them adversarially. A model can ace same-root clustering and still be blind to suffix *meaning* — that is Morpheus's own admitted failure. So pair the root-family test with its inverse: a same-root-DIFFERENT-suffix separation test (do 'evden' and 'eve' get distinguished?). High root-family MAP together with low same-root-different-suffix separation is the exact signature of a morph channel that will fail your morph_counterfactual negatives.

techniques.name: Morphological-level tokenization only pays off with a larger vocabulary budget
techniques.description: Morphological tokenizers are not a drop-in win at standard vocabulary sizes; their advantage grows with vocabulary size much faster than BPE/WordPiece's does. Budget vocabulary parameters accordingly.
techniques.evidence: Toraman et al. (ACM TALLIP 2023): under matched RoBERTa pretraining on Turkish OSCAR, the morphological tokenizer only reaches parity with BPE/WordPiece; increasing vocabulary size improves Morphological and Word-level tokenizers more than the de facto ones; recommended ~20% of model parameters in vocabulary for de facto tokenizers vs ~40% for the others.
techniques.applicability: A budgeting rule if you build or swap a tokenizer for the morph channel, and a reason to be suspicious of any small-vocab morphological tokenizer comparison. More importantly, this is the strongest matched-conditions evidence that better segmentation alone does not buy downstream quality — supporting the choice to inject morphology as a separate channel with its own contrastive objective rather than as a tokenizer swap in the semantic encoder.

techniques.name: Frozen-layer morphological feature probing (Case, Tense, Number, Voice, Mood, Aspect)
techniques.description: Train linear/MLP diagnostic classifiers on frozen encoder representations to predict UD morphological features, layer by layer, using BOUN/IMST gold annotations. Middle layers typically carry the most morphosyntactic signal.
techniques.evidence: Search results describe multilabel morphosyntactic probing (arXiv:2104.08464) and cross-lingual BERT morphology probing (arXiv:2004.03032), with Turkish probes scoring worst among the compared languages and mBERT layer 6 strongest overall; a Turkish baseline was reported with low per-feature scores for Voice, Mood, Aspect, Case, Tense, PronType. These are snippet-level numbers I did not read in the papers.
techniques.applicability: Gives you a per-feature map of which suffix types your candidate encoders already encode before any fine-tuning. Run it on BOUN, per layer, per feature. Use it to (a) choose which layers LoRA should target — probe-strong layers are where morphological signal already lives — and (b) decide which feature types deserve the most hard negatives in the synthesized eval set: put your synthesis budget on the features the encoders probe WORST, since those are where the fine-tuning has headroom.

techniques.name: Late-interaction (ColBERT-style) retrieval to preserve token-level morphological signal
techniques.description: Instead of collapsing a passage to one vector, keep per-token vectors and score with MaxSim, so a single morphologically decisive token can drive the match. Turkish ColBERT models exist and are trained via a two-stage pipeline: fine-tune an encoder on Turkish NLI/STS, then convert to ColBERT with PyLate on MS MARCO-TR.
techniques.evidence: TurkColBERT (arXiv:2511.16528, ACLing-2025 / Procedia Computer Science): 10 models across five Turkish BEIR datasets; late-interaction models consistently outperform dense encoders while being 3-5x smaller, with ColmmBERT-base-TR up to +13.8% mAP on domain-specific tasks; a 1.0M-param colbert-hash-nano-tr retains over 71% of the average mAP of the 600M turkish-e5-large. Snippet-level, not read in full.
techniques.applicability: Highly relevant to your eval set's design assumption. Your typed negatives differ from the gold positive by one suffix inside one word — a single mean-pooled vector is exactly the architecture most likely to wash that difference out. Worth adding a Turkish ColBERT model as a reference row in your selection matrix: if late interaction crushes dense encoders on your morph set, that is evidence the morphological signal is present in the tokens but destroyed by pooling, which would reframe your project from 'add a morph encoder' to 'stop pooling away morphology'.

techniques.name: Cheap non-neural floors: 5-character truncation and lemmatized BM25
techniques.description: Index Turkish documents by truncating every word to its first 5 characters (or by running a lemmatizer) and retrieve with BM25. Historically these are statistically indistinguishable from each other on Turkish ad hoc retrieval.
techniques.evidence: Can et al. (JASIST 2008), 408,305 documents and 72 queries: simple fixed-length truncation, corpus-statistics-based truncation, and an elaborate lemmatizer-based stemmer all give similar retrieval effectiveness. Reinforced 17 years later by MorphScore-70's finding that morphological alignment does not explain much variance in downstream performance.
techniques.applicability: Add both as baseline rows in your evaluation, especially on the held-out morph set. They are nearly free to compute and they make your claim falsifiable. They should score near-zero on your morph_counterfactual items by construction (truncation cannot distinguish 'evden' from 'eve'), and that gap is the cleanest possible demonstration that your eval set measures suffix *semantics* rather than the lexical-variant matching that classical Turkish IR already solved.

gaps: No published Turkish retrieval benchmark specifically targeting SUFFIX SEMANTICS. Everything I found is either lexical/root-level (Morpheus root-family MAP), grammatical acceptability (TurBLiMP), general retrieval (TR-MTEB, TurkColBERT, Turkish-BEIR), or morphological tagging (BOUN). A 50-query set where the distractors differ by one morpheme and the correct answer changes appears to be genuinely novel — this is a publishable contribution, not just an internal eval, and you should frame it that way.

No paper found that uses a SEPARATE morphological channel encoder fused with a semantic encoder for retrieval in any language, let alone Turkish. All the Turkish work I found modifies the single tokenizer/vocabulary of one model. Your architecture is unvalidated by prior work in both directions — no supporting evidence, but also no one has shown it fails.

No paper found on LoRA contrastive fine-tuning for Turkish morphological retrieval specifically. I found LoRA-free approaches (full pretraining, tokenizer surgery + distillation) but nothing combining parameter-efficient adaptation with a morphology-targeted contrastive objective for Turkish.

The direction of evidence on 'does morphology help' is genuinely contradictory and unresolved: Can et al. 2008 (truncation == lemmatizer), Toraman et al. 2023 (morphological tokenizer only reaches parity), and MorphScore-70 (alignment does not predict downstream) all point one way; Tokens with Meaning, Morpheus, HeceTokenizer and Altinok's affix-atomicity result point the other. Note that the 'morphology helps' papers are disproportionately 2026 single-author preprints with self-reported numbers, and the 'morphology does not help' papers are disproportionately peer-reviewed and use matched-condition controls. Weight accordingly.

I could not verify the MorphScore-70 correlation statistics (no R^2, no p-values, no Turkish-specific score obtained). The PDF fetch returned nothing usable and OpenReview was behind a bot check. This is the single most load-bearing negative claim in the survey — verify at arXiv:2507.06378 before citing it.

I could not read the full text of Çöltekin's 'Resources for Turkish NLP: A critical survey' (arXiv:2204.05042) — only the abstract page. Its documented quality problems with Turkish corpora and lexical resources are likely directly relevant to your eval-set QC and I have not captured them.

Pre-2015 accuracy numbers in this report (Sak et al. 96.80%/97.81% disambiguation; Ozen & Can 72% Turkish segmentation F-measure) come from search snippets and secondary citations, not from the papers. Verify any number you plan to put in a table.

Nuve (named in the task brief) returned no usable results in my searches — I found no paper, repository or evaluation for it. Either it is obscure enough to be irrelevant, or it needs a targeted search I did not run.
Turkish Penn Treebank: I found IMST (via METU-Sabancı) and BOUN with confidence, but did not confirm a distinct Turkish Penn treebank. Treat that item in the brief as unverified.

No evidence found on whether morphological signal survives mean-pooling in dual encoders — this is the mechanistic question underneath your whole architecture, and the TurkColBERT dense-vs-late-interaction gap is the closest available proxy. Worth an explicit experiment.

TURNA, VBART, Kanarya and TurkishBERTweet: I confirmed TURNA (1.1B UL2 encoder-decoder, Findings of ACL 2024, boun-tabi-LMG, outperforms multilingual models and competes with monolingual Turkish models on understanding) but found no morphology-specific analysis for any of them. None of these appear to have been evaluated on Turkish suffix semantics, so they are candidate backbones without morphological evidence either way.

SIGMORPHON Turkish specifics are thin: I confirmed Turkish was in the 2020 unsupervised paradigm completion task (3,095 train / 787 dev / 8,502 test instances) and that 2022 systems beat Morfessor2 by 30.71% absolute on sentence-level morpheme segmentation, but I did not verify whether Turkish was in the 2022 morpheme segmentation task or obtain Turkish-specific segmentation scores.

topic: fine-grained-negation: dense retrievers failing on meaning-flipping minimal contrasts (negation, exclusion, word order, instructions) and the fix recipes — read as an analogue for "one Turkish suffix flips the meaning"

papers.title: NevIR: Negation in Neural Information Retrieval
papers.why_relevant: The canonical demonstration that IR models ignore meaning-flipping edits. Task shape is exactly the team's: rank two documents that differ ONLY by negation, given two queries. This is the closest published analogue to a 'one suffix flips the meaning' eval.
papers.approach: Crowdsourced contrastive document pairs; pairwise evaluation (a model is correct only if it ranks BOTH queries correctly, so random = 25%). Compares bi-encoder, sparse, late-interaction, cross-encoder architectures.
papers.key_results: Abstract states most IR models perform similarly to or worse than random ranking; ordering is cross-encoders > late-interaction > bi-encoders/sparse. Continued fine-tuning on contrastive negation documents raises performance (as does model size) but a large gap to humans remains. I read these as claims in the abstract; the specific per-model numbers I have come from the reproduction paper below, not from this page.

papers.title: Reproducing NevIR: Negation in Neural Information Retrieval
papers.why_relevant: The single most useful paper for the team: it gives the actual numbers, tests whether fine-tuning fixes the problem, whether the fix TRANSFERS to a different fine-grained phenomenon (ExcluIR), and what it costs on general retrieval. Directly predicts the risks of the team's LoRA contrastive plan.
papers.approach: Re-runs NevIR across architectures, adds listwise LLM rerankers, then fine-tunes one model per architecture family on NevIR and on ExcluIR and cross-evaluates. Also tracks MS MARCO MRR@10 to measure collateral damage.
papers.key_results: Random = 25%. Reproduced pairwise accuracy: DPR 6.5, msmarco-bert-base-dot-v5 6.9, all-mpnet-base-v2 8.1, multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1 11.1; cross-encoders MonoT5-small 27.7, MonoT5-base 34.9, MonoT5-3B 50.6; listwise LLM rerankers Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 46.3, GPT-4o-mini 64.1, GPT-4o 70.1, o3-mini 77.3. After fine-tuning on NevIR: bi-encoder (multi-qa-mpnet) ~50%, cross-encoder (MonoT5-base) ~75%. Transfer: only the cross-encoder generalised between NevIR and ExcluIR; bi-encoders and listwise LLM rerankers improved only on the dataset they were trained on. Collateral damage: multi-qa-mpnet selected on NevIR alone dropped to 0.06 MRR@10 on MS MARCO vs 0.20 with a trade-off-based checkpoint criterion.

papers.title: ExcluIR: Exclusionary Neural Information Retrieval
papers.why_relevant: Second fine-grained phenomenon where a small lexical addition ('but not X') inverts which document is relevant. Provides both a benchmark AND a 70K training set — a template for how to build a train/eval split around a single contrast type.
papers.approach: Built on HotpotQA: ChatGPT generates an exclusionary query from two relevant documents such that only one contains the answer while the other is explicitly rejected. 3,452 manually annotated eval queries; 70,293 training queries each with one positive and one negative document.
papers.key_results: Abstract-level claims only: models across architectures struggle on exclusionary queries; adding the training data improves them but a gap to human performance remains; generative retrieval models have a natural advantage. No numeric table on the abstract page I fetched.

papers.title: CONDAQA: A Contrastive Reading Comprehension Dataset for Reasoning about Negation
papers.why_relevant: The construction methodology is directly copyable for the team's larger synthesized eval set: for each passage, crowdworkers produce a CLUSTER of edits (paraphrase the negation, change its scope, reverse it) so a model cannot shortcut. And they score CLUSTER-level consistency, not per-item accuracy — a much harder and more honest metric than plain nDCG.
papers.approach: 14,182 QA pairs, 200+ unique negation cues; three edit types per passage (paraphrase / scope change / polarity reversal) forming contrast clusters; consistency metric requires getting the whole cluster right.
papers.key_results: Reported in search results: best model (UNIFIEDQA-v2-3B) reaches 42% on the consistency metric vs 81% human. I did not fetch the paper itself, so treat these two numbers as snippet-sourced.

papers.title: Language models are not naysayers: An analysis of language models on negation benchmarks
papers.why_relevant: Establishes that the failure is not a small-model artifact — scaling autoregressive LMs does not solve negation. Useful framing for why a bigger Turkish base encoder alone will not buy morphological sensitivity.
papers.approach: Systematic evaluation of GPT-neo / GPT-3 / InstructGPT across model sizes and prompts on a suite of existing negation benchmarks.
papers.key_results: Qualitative findings reported: insensitivity to the presence of negation, inability to capture the lexical semantics of negation, failure to reason under negation. No numbers verified by me.

papers.title: Making Language Models Robust Against Negation
papers.why_relevant: The cheapest fix recipe in this whole survey: a self-supervised pretraining objective that needs NO labels and no synthetic data, only raw corpora. Trivially portable to Turkish because the negation cue (-ma/-me, değil, -sIz) is detectable by a morphological analyzer or regex.
papers.approach: Next Sentence Polarity Prediction (NSPP): given only the first of two consecutive sentences, predict whether the next sentence contains a negation cue. Plus a negation-aware variant of NSP. Further-pretrain BERT/RoBERTa on this.
papers.key_results: Search-result claim: models further pretrained on these tasks beat off-the-shelf versions on nine negation-related benchmarks, with 1.8%–9.1% improvement on CondaQA. Not verified against the PDF.

papers.title: Learning Robust Negation Text Representations
papers.why_relevant: The closest published thing to what the team is about to do: LLM-distill a synthetic contrastive dataset targeting one semantic phenomenon, fine-tune a sentence encoder on it, and check that general benchmark performance survives. Also notable that they include HEDGING alongside negation — i.e. graded, not binary, meaning shifts.
papers.approach: Distil data from LLMs using diverse linguistics-grounded patterns of negation and hedging; fine-tune a strong BERT-based text encoder with a standard contrastive objective; also adapted to LLMs.
papers.key_results: Abstract claims large improvement in negation understanding while remaining competitive on general benchmarks. IMPORTANT: my PDF extraction produced a tidy results table (NevIR/ExcluIR/CondaQA/MTEB) that I could not corroborate and that looked model-generated, so I am deliberately reporting NO numbers for this paper. Read the PDF directly before citing figures.

papers.title: This is not correct! Negation-aware Evaluation of Language Generation Systems (NegBLEURT / CANNOT dataset)
papers.why_relevant: Demonstrates the RULE-BASED counterfactual route as an alternative to LLM synthesis: they wrote a sentence negation tool and mass-produced contrast pairs from it. Turkish is far better suited to this than English — a morphological analyzer (Zemberek/TRmorph) can flip -ma/-me, tense, case or possessive deterministically and label the edit type for free.
papers.approach: Rule-based sentence negation tool → CANNOT dataset (reported as 77,376 samples, roughly half negated pairs and half paraphrase pairs) → fine-tune a sentence transformer and a BLEURT-style metric for negation sensitivity.
papers.key_results: Claim from search results: learned metrics based on LMs underestimate how much negation changes meaning; fine-tuning on CANNOT improves negation sensitivity. Dataset size 77,376 is snippet-sourced (GitHub dmlls/cannot-dataset).

papers.title: Revisiting subword tokenization: A case study on affixal negation in large language models
papers.why_relevant: The only paper I found that directly studies MORPHOLOGICAL (affixal) rather than lexical negation in relation to tokenization — i.e. the team's exact hypothesis that a suffix-aware tokenizer is needed. Its conclusion is a useful counterweight to that hypothesis.
papers.approach: Evaluate LLMs with different subword tokenizers on affixal negation (negation carried by a bound morpheme), correlating tokenization quality with negation sensitivity.
papers.key_results: Reported conclusion: there are mismatches between tokenization accuracy and negation-detection performance, but on the whole models reliably recognize the meaning of affixal negation. Implication for the team: morphologically implausible tokenization is NOT automatically the cause of morphological insensitivity — measure it, don't assume it.

papers.title: INSTRUCTIR: A Benchmark for Instruction Following of Information Retrieval Models
papers.why_relevant: Instruction-following retrieval is the same failure mode wearing different clothes: a short piece of text that should re-rank everything gets treated as extra keywords. Their instance-wise instruction design is the template for 'the suffix should change which document wins'.
papers.approach: Reformulates queries in existing retrieval datasets by attaching user-aligned, per-instance instructions; measures robustness to instruction variation.
papers.key_results: None verified.

papers.title: FollowIR: Evaluating and Teaching Information Retrieval Models to Follow Instructions
papers.why_relevant: Gives the right METRIC design for 'a small textual change should flip relevance': p-MRR is computed pairwise over documents whose relevance changed when the instruction changed. That is exactly how the team should score a morphological eval set — measure the DELTA in ranking induced by the suffix flip, not absolute nDCG.
papers.approach: Built from TREC narratives; altered instructions with known relevance consequences; pairwise p-MRR metric. Training set built by taking TREC narratives held out of the benchmark and using GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106 to synthesize relevant and irrelevant documents; FollowIR-7B fine-tuned from Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 with LoRA.
papers.key_results: Abstract-level: existing retrieval models fail to use instructions correctly, treating them as basic keywords; FollowIR-7B shows significant improvement after fine-tuning. Specific p-MRR values were not present on the abstract page and my PDF fetch was unreadable. The LoRA + GPT-synthesized-document training detail came from a search snippet.

papers.title: Towards Better Instruction Following Retrieval Models (InF-IR)
papers.why_relevant: Most directly transferable synthesis recipe for the team's upcoming LLM-generated dataset: build positives, then produce hard negatives by deliberately CORRUPTING one component (they corrupt the instruction and the query), then have a reasoning model verify each negative is plausible-but-wrong. Swap 'instruction' for 'morphological feature' and this is the team's pipeline.
papers.approach: InF-IR corpus: 38K+ expressive (instruction, query, document) triplets as positives; for each positive, two additional hard negatives generated by 'poisoning' the instruction and the query; all negatives validated by o3-mini for semantic plausibility while remaining instructionally incorrect. Explicitly designed so encoder-only embedding models (not just rerankers) can train on it.
papers.key_results: None verified.

papers.title: When and Why Vision-Language Models Behave Like Bags-of-Words, and What to Do About It? (ARO benchmark, NegCLIP)
papers.language_focus: English (vision-language, but the lesson is about the text tower)
papers.why_relevant: The canonical 'contrastively trained encoders are bags of words' result, and — more importantly — the canonical FIX: NegCLIP puts the minimally-perturbed negative in the same batch as the positive so the contrastive loss is forced to separate them. This is the exact mechanism the team needs for morphological counterfactuals, and it is architecture-agnostic.
papers.approach: ARO benchmark (Attribution, Relation, Order; 50,000+ test cases) probing relational, attributive and word-order understanding. NegCLIP fine-tunes with (a) nearest-neighbour hard negative IMAGES in-batch and (b) hard negative CAPTIONS made by perturbing word order of true captions.
papers.key_results: Search-result claims: models show severe lack of order sensitivity; NegCLIP improves ARO+CREPE by more than 10% over standard CLIP fine-tuning on 11 of 16 cases, without significant loss on standard downstream tasks. Snippet-sourced, not read in the paper.

papers.title: SugarCrepe: Fixing Hackable Benchmarks for Vision-Language Compositionality
papers.why_relevant: The single most important cautionary paper for the team's plan to SYNTHESIZE a larger morphological eval set with an LLM.
