Template- or LLM-generated hard negatives carry distributional artifacts (implausibility, fluency drop) that let a model win without ever comparing to the query — so the benchmark measures artifact detection, not morphological sensitivity.
papers.approach: Diagnose bias by showing 'blind' models with no access to the image beat state-of-the-art VLMs on existing compositionality benchmarks. Then regenerate negatives with LLMs (fluent, sensical) plus an adversarial refinement mechanism that maximally reduces the remaining bias.
papers.key_results: Abstract-level: blind models outperform SOTA vision-language models on prior benchmarks; on SugarCrepe, previously reported improvements from compositionality methods were 'hugely overestimated'. No numbers on the abstract page.

papers.title: NV-Retriever: Improving text embedding models with effective hard-negative mining
papers.why_relevant: Hard-negative mining is where the team's morphological counterfactuals will actually live, and this paper supplies the safety valve: a mined 'hard negative' is very often a FALSE negative. For Turkish this is acute — a suffix-flipped variant may still be a perfectly relevant document (e.g. a case or possessive change that does not alter topical relevance).
papers.approach: Positive-aware hard-negative mining: threshold candidate negatives against the score of the known positive. TopK-MarginPos (max negative score = positive score minus an absolute margin) and TopK-PercPos (negatives must score below a percentage of the positive's score).
papers.key_results: Search-result claims: on MS MARCO roughly 70% of the passages most similar to a query should arguably be labelled positive; TopK-MarginPos and TopK-PercPos perform best; a 95% threshold (retain a negative only if its similarity is below 95% of the positive's) was the optimal ablation setting. Snippet-sourced.

papers.title: Thunder-KoNUBench: A Corpus-Aligned Benchmark for Korean Negation Understanding
papers.authors_short: Jung, So, Lee, Kim, Ahn, Lee (SNU)
papers.language_focus: Korean (agglutinative) — closest typological analogue to Turkish I found
papers.why_relevant: The only benchmark I found that handles negation in an agglutinative language with an explicit morphological typology of negation forms — short-form vs long-form vs prohibitive, syntactic vs lexical — and that is corpus-aligned (frequency of each type measured in real text rather than uniformly sampled). This is the design the team should copy for Turkish -ma/-me vs değil vs -sIz vs yok. Note also that Thunder-NUBench (the English original, Findings of EACL 2026, arXiv 2506.14397) reports multilingual instruction tuning DEGRADING negation performance in Korean — a warning for multilingual Turkish encoders.
papers.approach: Corpus analysis of 29,476 Korean sentences found 3,160 negative instances (10.7% prevalence), used to set the type distribution. 4,784 instances (2,500 train / 1,000 val / 1,284 test). Four-way multiple choice: standard negation (correct) vs LOCAL negation vs contradiction vs paraphrase — i.e. typed distractors, exactly like the team's morph_counterfactual / partial_trap / state_variant typology. Human-authored negation options, API-generated then manually refined contradiction/paraphrase options, cross-reviewed.
papers.key_results: Zero-shot over 47 models: Korean-specialised models averaged 62.8% (symbol setting), non-Korean models 62.7% — i.e. language-specific pretraining bought essentially nothing. Human baseline 97.6% (range 88.0–100.0). Over 90% of cloze-setting errors were concentrated on the LOCAL-negation distractor (the partial/scope trap), not the easy ones. Fine-tuning improved scores by 34.2% (cloze) and 30.7% (symbol). Cloze-style supervision transferred to symbol format better (+10.5%) than the reverse (+6.4%).

techniques.name: Paired/pairwise scoring instead of nDCG (NevIR pairwise accuracy, FollowIR p-MRR)
techniques.description: Do not score a fine-grained contrast set with nDCG@10 against a big corpus. NevIR scores a model correct only if it ranks the gold document above its counterfactual for BOTH queries in the pair — which sets the random baseline at 25%, not 50%, and kills the ability to score well by topical similarity alone. FollowIR's p-MRR instead measures the ranking DELTA induced by the perturbation, averaged over exactly those documents whose relevance status changed.
techniques.applicability: The team's 50-query set (1 gold + typed negatives each) should be scored as (a) pairwise accuracy per negative TYPE with the correct random baseline stated, and (b) a delta metric: how much does the ranking move when the suffix flips. Report per-type breakdown — Thunder-KoNUBench found >90% of errors concentrated on a single distractor type (local/partial negation), which an aggregate score would have hidden. Their existing 'partial_trap' type is the analogue and is probably where all the signal is.
techniques.evidence: NevIR (EACL 2024) pairwise construction, random = 25% per the reproduction paper; FollowIR p-MRR is computed pairwise over relevance-changed documents (arXiv 2403.15246).

techniques.name: In-batch minimal-pair contrastive negatives (NegCLIP recipe)
techniques.description: For each anchor, place its minimally-perturbed counterfactual in the SAME batch as the positive, so the InfoNCE denominator is dominated by a document that differs by one edit. Nothing else in the batch forces the encoder to encode the edit; only the co-located minimal pair does.
techniques.applicability: Direct blueprint for the LoRA contrastive fine-tune: batches of (query, gold passage, suffix-flipped passage) where the flipped passage is guaranteed in-batch. Worth doing on both channels — semantic encoder and morph channel encoder — and worth also including word-order-perturbed negatives, which is what NegCLIP used for the order dimension.
techniques.evidence: NegCLIP (ICLR 2023) reports >10% gains on 11 of 16 ARO+CREPE cases over standard CLIP fine-tuning without significant downstream loss (snippet-sourced, not read in-paper).

techniques.name: Rule-based morphological counterfactual generation (CANNOT-style) as a precision backbone for LLM synthesis
techniques.description: CANNOT built ~77K contrast pairs with a rule-based sentence negation tool rather than an LLM. The advantages are that the edit type is known by construction, the edit is guaranteed minimal, and there is no LLM stylistic drift between positive and negative.
techniques.applicability: Turkish is far more amenable to this than English: a morphological analyzer/generator (Zemberek, TRmorph) can deterministically flip verbal negation (-ma/-me), tense, aspect, case, possessive and privative -sIz, producing typed, minimal, guaranteed-well-formed negatives at scale — and the type label falls out for free, which is exactly what the eval set's typed-negative schema needs. Recommendation: use the rule-based generator for the CONTROLLED axis and the LLM only for naturalizing context, not for choosing the edit.
techniques.evidence: CANNOT / NegBLEURT (INLG 2023); dataset size and rule-based tool are snippet-sourced from the paper page and GitHub repo.

techniques.name: Query-blind (shortcut) auditing of a synthesized eval set
techniques.description: SugarCrepe's diagnostic: run a model that CANNOT see the query and check whether it can still pick the gold document. If it can, the benchmark is measuring generation artifacts (implausibility, fluency, length, LLM phrasing tics), not the phenomenon. They then regenerated negatives with an LLM plus an adversarial refinement loop that minimizes the residual bias.
techniques.applicability: Mandatory before scaling the 50-query set to thousands with an LLM. Concretely: (1) score every candidate with a Turkish LM's perplexity and reject negatives that are systematically less fluent than golds; (2) train/score a query-blind classifier on gold-vs-negative and require it to be near chance; (3) check length and surface-overlap distributions match. Without this, a big LLM-synthesized Turkish morph set will likely be hackable, and any fine-tuning gain measured on it will be overstated — SugarCrepe's exact finding.
techniques.evidence: SugarCrepe (NeurIPS 2023 D&B): blind models with no image access beat SOTA vision-language models on prior benchmarks; re-evaluation showed prior improvements were hugely overestimated.

techniques.name: Reasoning-model validation of every synthesized hard negative
techniques.description: InF-IR generates hard negatives by deliberately corrupting one component of a positive triplet, then passes each candidate to a strong reasoning model that must confirm it is semantically plausible yet genuinely non-satisfying. Negatives that fail either test are dropped.
techniques.applicability: Second gate after the query-blind audit, and the one that catches the specifically Turkish failure: an LLM asked to 'flip the suffix' will sometimes produce a form that is a paraphrase (still relevant) or ungrammatical (trivially rejectable). A verifier prompt that asks 'does this still answer the query? is it well-formed Turkish? which feature changed?' turns silent label noise into a rejected row. Have the verifier also EMIT the negative type, then cross-check against the generator's intended type — disagreement is a strong noise signal.
techniques.evidence: InF-IR / Towards Better Instruction Following Retrieval Models (arXiv 2505.21439): 38K+ positive triplets, two poisoned hard negatives each, validated by o3-mini (snippet-sourced).

techniques.name: Positive-aware false-negative filtering on mined negatives
techniques.description: Threshold mined negatives against the positive's own score rather than taking top-k blindly: TopK-MarginPos (keep negatives scoring below positive_score − margin) or TopK-PercPos (below a percentage of positive_score, ~95% optimal in their ablation).
techniques.applicability: Critical for the morphological channel, where the false-negative rate is structurally high: many single-suffix edits (case, possessive, plural) do NOT change topical relevance, so a naively mined 'morphological hard negative' is often a true positive. Apply the percentile filter to mined negatives, and keep the deliberately constructed counterfactuals in a separate, human/LLM-verified bucket that bypasses the filter.
techniques.evidence: NV-Retriever (arXiv 2407.15831): ~70% of MS MARCO's most-similar passages arguably deserve a positive label; TopK-MarginPos/TopK-PercPos best, 95% threshold optimal (snippet-sourced).

techniques.name: Contrastive EDIT CLUSTERS with all-or-nothing consistency scoring
techniques.description: CondaQA builds, for every source item, a cluster of edits: paraphrase the negated statement, change the SCOPE of the negation, and reverse the negation. A model is credited only if it handles the whole cluster. This removes the shortcut of latching onto the presence of a negation cue instead of its semantics.
techniques.applicability: The team already has typed negatives (morph_counterfactual, same_feature_wrong_content, partial_trap, state_variant), which is halfway there — the missing piece is (a) an explicit PARAPHRASE edit where the morphology changes but the meaning does NOT (a suffix change that should be ignored), and (b) cluster-level consistency as the headline metric. Without the paraphrase arm, a model can score well by simply becoming hypersensitive to any suffix change, which would wreck ordinary Turkish retrieval where morphological variants of the same root must still match.
techniques.evidence: CONDAQA (EMNLP 2022): three edit types per passage; best model 42% cluster consistency vs 81% human (snippet-sourced).

techniques.name: Self-supervised polarity/cue-prediction pretraining before contrastive fine-tuning
techniques.description: Next Sentence Polarity Prediction: given the first of two consecutive sentences, predict whether the next one contains a negation cue — requires only raw text and no labels. A sibling technique is negation-focused pretraining (Truong et al., NAACL 2022), which always masks negation cues so the MLM objective is forced to model them.
techniques.applicability: Ideal cheap pre-step for the MORPH CHANNEL encoder, which is meant to be lightweight and suffix-sensitive. Turkish version: mask the inflectional suffix chain (identified by a morphological analyzer) and predict it, and/or predict whether the following sentence carries -ma/-me/değil/-sIz. Uses only a Turkish corpus, needs no synthesized data, and can be run before the expensive contrastive stage. Generalises beyond negation to any morphological feature the team cares about.
techniques.evidence: Making Language Models Robust Against Negation (NAACL 2025) reports 1.8%–9.1% improvement on CondaQA and gains on nine negation benchmarks from NSPP further-pretraining (snippet-sourced).

techniques.name: Architecture triage: expect the bi-encoder to be the weakest link
techniques.description: On NevIR the ordering is consistent and stark: cross-encoders > late-interaction > bi-encoders/sparse, with bi-encoders far BELOW random. A single pooled vector appears to be structurally poor at representing 'same topic, opposite polarity'.
techniques.applicability: A pure dual-encoder may have a ceiling on the morphological eval set no amount of LoRA fully removes. Two hedges worth budgeting for: (1) a late-interaction / ColBERT-style Turkish model (TurkColBERT exists as a benchmark reference) for the morph channel, where token-level matching can see the suffix; (2) a small cross-encoder reranker over the dual-encoder's top-k for the fine-grained decision. Also relevant: fine-tuned bi-encoders in the NevIR reproduction did NOT transfer across contrast types, while the cross-encoder did.
techniques.evidence: Reproducing NevIR (arXiv 2502.13506, fetched): DPR 6.5 / all-mpnet 8.1 / multi-qa-mpnet 11.1 vs random 25; MonoT5-3B 50.6; only the cross-encoder generalised between NevIR and ExcluIR.

techniques.name: Joint checkpoint selection: morph accuracy AND general retrieval, never morph alone
techniques.description: Selecting the fine-tuning checkpoint by the fine-grained metric alone catastrophically overfits. The reproduction paper shows the same model at 0.06 MRR@10 on MS MARCO under NevIR-only selection versus 0.20 under a trade-off criterion — a ~3x collateral loss purely from the selection rule.
techniques.applicability: Maps onto the repo's existing Section E weighted selection matrix: the same joint-criterion logic should govern LoRA checkpoint selection, not just base-model choice. Concretely, evaluate every checkpoint on both the morph eval set and Turkish-BEIR/TR-MTEB nDCG@10, and select on the joint score. Given the notebook already computes own_ndcg10 and morph_acc, this is close to free.
techniques.evidence: Reproducing NevIR (fetched): multi-qa-mpnet 0.06 MRR@10 (NevIR-only selection) vs 0.20 MRR@10 (trade-off criterion) on MS MARCO.

techniques.name: Train on a MIXTURE of contrast types, not one
techniques.description: Fine-tuning on one fine-grained phenomenon does not reliably transfer to another: in the NevIR reproduction, bi-encoders and listwise LLM rerankers improved only on the dataset they were trained on; only the cross-encoder generalised between NevIR and ExcluIR. Separately, cloze-style supervision transferred to a different answer format better than the reverse in Thunder-KoNUBench.
techniques.applicability: Do not train only on verbal negation (-ma/-me) and expect case, tense, possessive or privative sensitivity to follow — for a bi-encoder the evidence says it will not. Stratify the synthesized training set across every morphological feature the eval set contains, and hold out at least one feature entirely to measure cross-feature transfer honestly. Also asymmetric-transfer-aware: train in the harder/freer format.
techniques.evidence: Reproducing NevIR cross-dataset fine-tuning results (fetched); Thunder-KoNUBench asymmetric transfer +10.5% vs +6.4% (fetched).

techniques.name: Corpus-aligned type distribution for the eval set
techniques.description: Thunder-KoNUBench set its distribution of negation types by first measuring real corpus frequency (29,476 sentences analysed, 3,160 negative instances, 10.7% prevalence) rather than sampling types uniformly. This keeps the benchmark predictive of deployed behaviour instead of over-weighting rare constructions.
techniques.applicability: Before generating thousands of Turkish morphological queries, measure how often each feature actually appears in the target retrieval corpus (a search snippet from the TrGLUE/SentiTurca paper reports verbal -ma/-me negation in 11.75% of finite verbs, which is a plausible starting reference — verify against the paper). Weight the synthesized set toward what real Turkish queries and documents actually do, and report per-type results separately so a rare-but-hard type cannot be averaged away.
techniques.evidence: Thunder-KoNUBench (fetched): 10.7% negative-instance prevalence used to align the benchmark; TrGLUE 11.75% figure is snippet-sourced and unverified.

techniques.name: Include a hedging / graded axis, not just binary flips
techniques.description: The Learning Robust Negation Text Representations recipe deliberately covers hedging patterns ('might', 'could') alongside outright negation — i.e. the meaning shift is graded, not binary.
techniques.applicability: Turkish has rich grammatical machinery for exactly this: the evidential/reportative -mIş, the abilitative -Abil, the conditional -sA, and the optative. These change epistemic status without flipping polarity, and are plausibly harder for an embedding model than -ma/-me. Worth adding as a distinct negative type alongside the existing state_variant category — it is the axis most likely to be missing from a set that started from negation.
techniques.evidence: Learning Robust Negation Text Representations (arXiv 2507.12782) abstract explicitly names diverse patterns of negation AND hedging. No numbers reported by me for this paper (see the paper entry's caveat).

gaps: No Turkish — and as far as I can find, no agglutinative-language — equivalent of NevIR or ExcluIR exists for RETRIEVAL. Thunder-KoNUBench (Korean) is the closest typological analogue but it is a multiple-choice LLM benchmark, not a ranking benchmark. The team's morph eval set may genuinely be the first of its kind for Turkish retrieval, which is a publishable angle but also means no external baseline to calibrate against.

Essentially all negation-IR work targets LEXICAL negation (the word 'not', 'but not X'). Morphological/affixal negation appears in exactly one paper I found (Truong et al., NAACL 2024) and only for LLM detection, never for retrieval. The gap between 'model detects affixal negation' and 'retriever's embedding space separates affixally-negated documents' is unmeasured everywhere.

I found no published measurement of whether Turkish or multilingual embedding models fail on single-suffix flips. TR-MTEB, TurkColBERT and the Turkish-BEIR ports do not test it. So the team has no prior on the effect size — the pilot probe in notebook Section C is currently the only evidence, and it is 50 triplets.

No paper I found reports the effect of negation/fine-grained contrastive fine-tuning on general retrieval performance IN A MORPHOLOGICALLY RICH LANGUAGE. The one hard number on this trade-off (0.06 vs 0.20 MRR@10) is English MS MARCO. Whether hypersensitising a Turkish encoder to suffixes damages ordinary morphological-variant matching (where suffix differences SHOULD be ignored) is completely untested and is, in my view, the team's largest technical risk.

No LoRA-specific numbers for negation/fine-grained robustness. FollowIR-7B used LoRA but I could not verify its p-MRR delta from the sources I could read. Whether low-rank adaptation has enough capacity to install a fine-grained polarity distinction — versus needing full fine-tuning or a separate channel — is unanswered in what I surveyed.

Nobody publishes a per-negative-TYPE breakdown for retrieval. Thunder-KoNUBench does it for multiple choice (>90% of errors on one distractor type) and the finding is dramatic; no IR paper I saw does the equivalent. The team is well positioned to be the first, and should expect the aggregate number to be misleading.

There is no standard metric for 'morphological sensitivity' in retrieval. The candidates I found are borrowed: NevIR pairwise accuracy, FollowIR p-MRR, CondaQA cluster consistency. The team will have to pick and justify one — I would argue for pairwise accuracy per type plus cluster consistency including a meaning-PRESERVING morphological edit as a control.

The reliability of LLM-synthesized morphological counterfactuals in Turkish is unvalidated. SugarCrepe's finding that LLM/template negatives are hackable was established for English vision-language captions; nobody has checked whether GPT-class models produce artifact-free minimal morphological edits in Turkish. Given Turkish generation quality is weaker than English in most frontier models, the artifact risk is probably HIGHER here, not lower.

I could not extract verified numeric results from Learning Robust Negation Text Representations (2507.12782), the closest methodological precedent to the team's plan — no arXiv HTML version exists and PDF extraction was unreliable. Someone should read that PDF manually before the team commits to a synthesis recipe.

ExcluIR's actual numeric results and FollowIR's p-MRR table both eluded me (abstract-only and unreadable PDF respectively), so the quantitative claim 'training data helps but a human gap remains' is qualitative in my report for those two.
confidence: Mixed, and I want to be precise about where. HIGH confidence, read directly from full text: all numbers attributed to 'Reproducing NevIR' (arXiv 2502.13506 HTML) and to Thunder-KoNUBench (arXiv 2601.04693 HTML) — those two I fetched and read properly, and they carry most of the quantitative weight of this report. MEDIUM confidence, abstract-level only: NevIR, ExcluIR, FollowIR, SugarCrepe, Learning Robust Negation Text Representations — I fetched these pages but they were abstracts, so I report their claims and not numbers they did not state. LOWER confidence, search-snippet only: CondaQA's 42%/81%, the NSPP 1.8-9.1% CondaQA range, NegCLIP's '>10% on 11/16 cases', NV-Retriever's 70%-false-negative and 95%-threshold figures, CANNOT's 77,376 size, and the TrGLUE 11.75% Turkish negation frequency. Each of those is flagged in-place; verify before citing in a writeup. ONE EXPLICIT NON-REPORT: a PDF extraction of arXiv 2507.12782 returned a clean NevIR/ExcluIR/CondaQA/MTEB results table with suspiciously round approximate values; I judged it likely fabricated by the extraction model and have deliberately omitted those numbers rather than pass them through. Do not let that table resurface from anywhere without reading the actual PDF. On coverage: I ran 14 searches and 10 fetches; several arXiv PDFs (FollowIR, SugarCrepe, the counterfactual dense-retrieval paper 2412.20756) were unreadable through the fetch tool, so a manual read of those three would meaningfully upgrade the quantitative picture. Also note two structural biases in this literature that shape my conclusions: it is overwhelmingly English, and it is overwhelmingly about LEXICAL rather than morphological contrast — so the transfer of every fix recipe here to Turkish suffix flips is my inference, not any paper's demonstrated claim.

topic: Contrastive fine-tuning recipes for text embedding models, focused on what transfers to LoRA fine-tuning a Turkish dual-encoder retriever with morphological hard negatives

papers.title: SimCSE: Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings
papers.approach: Unsupervised variant uses dropout as the only augmentation (same sentence twice through the encoder = positive pair). Supervised variant uses NLI entailment pairs as positives and contradiction pairs as explicit hard negatives inside the InfoNCE denominator. Framed via alignment (positives close) and uniformity (embeddings spread on the hypersphere).
papers.key_results: Search snippets report 76.3 avg Spearman (unsupervised BERT-base) and 81.6 (supervised BERT-base) on STS, described as +4.2 / +2.2 over prior best. I did not fetch the PDF to confirm these.
papers.why_relevant: The origin of the 'one explicitly typed hard negative per anchor' training format that your morph_counterfactual / partial_trap negatives slot directly into. Also the source of the alignment-vs-uniformity vocabulary you will need to explain why a morph-sensitive space does not collapse.

papers.title: Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (E5)
papers.approach: Two-stage: (1) weakly-supervised contrastive pre-training on a large curated web text-pair corpus (CCPairs) using InfoNCE with in-batch negatives only; (2) supervised fine-tuning on a small amount of high-quality labeled data. Introduces the query:/passage: prefix convention.
papers.key_results: Snippets state E5 is the first model to beat BM25 on BEIR zero-shot without labeled data, and that fine-tuned E5 beat models 40x larger on MTEB. Numbers not individually verified.
papers.why_relevant: Canonical two-stage template. For your project the mapping is: stage 1 = broad Turkish pair data (cheap, in-batch negatives only), stage 2 = the small, expensive, LLM-synthesized morphological triplet set with explicit typed negatives. Also the origin of the prompt-prefix bug your CLAUDE.md already warns about.

papers.title: Multilingual E5 Text Embeddings: A Technical Report
papers.approach: Same two-stage recipe as E5 applied to XLM-R backbones. Stage 1: InfoNCE with in-batch negatives only, batch size 32,768, 30,000 steps (~1B pairs seen per search snippets). Stage 2: supervised fine-tuning adding mined hard negatives plus knowledge distillation from a cross-encoder/teacher.
papers.key_results: Batch 32768 / 30k steps figure came from a search snippet, not a fetched page. Temperature value not stated in what I read.
papers.why_relevant: This is almost certainly the family your semantic encoder baseline sits in, and it establishes the asymmetry you should copy: huge batch + in-batch-only negatives first, then small batch + curated hard negatives + distillation. The distillation step is a cheap way to keep general Turkish retrieval from regressing while you inject morphology.

papers.title: Towards General Text Embeddings with Multi-stage Contrastive Learning (GTE)
papers.approach: Multi-stage contrastive learning over a large heterogeneous mixture of relevance pairs: unsupervised contrastive pre-training then supervised fine-tuning, with an emphasis on scaling and mixing data sources rather than architectural tricks. BERT-based, 110M-330M params.
papers.key_results: Snippets claim gte-base (110M) outperforms the OpenAI embedding API and some 10x larger models on MTEB. Not verified against the PDF.
papers.why_relevant: Evidence that a small BERT-scale encoder trained with good data mixing is competitive, which is relevant to the lightweight morphological channel encoder: it does not need to be an LLM. Also the strongest argument for data-mixture balancing over loss engineering.

papers.title: BGE M3-Embedding: Multi-Lingual, Multi-Functionality, Multi-Granularity Text Embeddings Through Self-Knowledge Distillation
papers.authors_short: Chen, Xiao, Zhang, Luo, Lian, Liu
papers.approach: Single model producing dense, sparse (lexical) and multi-vector (ColBERT-style) scores simultaneously; the three scoring functions are ensembled into a teacher signal and distilled back into each individual head (self-knowledge distillation). Supports up to 8192 tokens.
papers.key_results: Claims SOTA on multilingual/cross-lingual retrieval at time of publication. I read only the abstract-level description.
papers.why_relevant: The self-knowledge-distillation trick is the closest published analogue to your dual-channel design: instead of two separate encoders, BGE-M3 gets a lexical/sparse channel and a semantic channel out of one trunk and reconciles them by distillation. If your morph channel and semantic channel are to be fused at scoring time, this is the reference architecture for how to train them jointly without one channel dominating.

papers.title: Qwen3 Embedding: Advancing Text Embedding and Reranking Through Foundation Models
papers.approach: Three stages: (1) weakly-supervised pre-training on ~150M synthetic pairs generated by Qwen3-32B; (2) supervised fine-tuning on ~7M labeled plus ~12M synthetic pairs filtered to cosine similarity > 0.7; (3) model merging via spherical linear interpolation (slerp) over checkpoints saved during SFT. Loss is an extended InfoNCE whose denominator includes the positive, K hard negatives, in-batch query-query, in-batch doc-doc, and cross-pair query-doc similarities. Explicit false-negative mask: a candidate is masked out (m_ij = 0) if s_ij > s(q_i, d_i+) + 0.1, or if the candidate is the positive itself. Instruction format: "{Instruction} {Query}<|endoftext|>". MRL-style custom output dims: 1024 (0.6B), 2560 (4B), 4096 (8B).
papers.key_results: The masking rule and the 0.1 margin, the ~150M / ~7M / ~12M data sizes, the 0.7 cosine filter, and the per-size dimensions were read directly off the fetched HTML. Temperature value and batch size were NOT stated in the section I read.
papers.why_relevant: The single most directly copyable artifact here is the false-negative mask s_ij > s_pos + 0.1. That exact rule is also the one most likely to misfire on your data: a morph_counterfactual negative is lexically near-identical to the positive and will often score above s_pos + 0.1, so a naive port would silently delete precisely the negatives you built the dataset for. Plan to exempt curated typed negatives from the mask and apply it only to mined ones.

papers.title: NV-Embed: Improved Techniques for Training LLMs as Generalist Embedding Models
papers.approach: Decoder-only LLM turned into an embedder by (a) removing the causal attention mask during contrastive training to get bidirectional context, (b) a latent attention pooling layer (reported as 512 latents, 8 heads) instead of mean/last-token pooling, and (c) two-stage contrastive instruction tuning: stage 1 on retrieval data with in-batch negatives plus curated hard negatives; stage 2 blends in non-retrieval tasks and turns the in-batch-negative trick OFF.
papers.key_results: Reported as topping MTEB at publication time; I did not fetch the paper, so I have no verified table numbers.
papers.why_relevant: Two transferable ideas. First, pooling choice is a real lever, worth testing latent-attention or attention pooling for the morph channel where the discriminative signal lives in a few suffix subword positions that mean-pooling washes out. Second, the stage-2 'disable in-batch negatives when mixing task types' rule matters for you: mixing morph triplets and general retrieval pairs in one batch means in-batch negatives cross task boundaries and become meaningless or actively false.

papers.title: NV-Retriever: Improving text embedding models with effective hard-negative mining
papers.approach: Systematic ablation of hard-negative mining. Taxonomy: naive Top-K; TopK-Abs (drop negatives above an absolute score); TopK-MarginPos (threshold = positive score minus a margin); TopK-PercPos (threshold = a percentage of the positive score); plus sampling variants and Top-K-shifted-by-N.
papers.key_results: Read directly off the fetched HTML: best settings were TopK-PercPos at 95% of the positive score, TopK-MarginPos at margin 0.05, TopK-Abs at 0.7, Top-K-shifted at N=10. On e5-large-unsupervised across NQ/HotpotQA/FiQA, naive Top-K gave 0.5407 avg nDCG@10 vs 0.5856 for TopK-PercPos(95%): NQ 0.5445 -> 0.6369, HotpotQA 0.6120 -> 0.6414, FiQA 0.4658 -> 0.4784. Mistral-7B base with 1 hard negative reached 0.6479 avg with TopK-PercPos. Mining-model ablation: e5-mistral-7b-instruct best (0.5810), BM25 worst (0.5002). Ensembling 4 mining models gave only 0.5825 vs 0.5810. Ablations used 4 hard negatives/query; the released model used 1 hard negative in stage 1 and 5 in stage 2. Training config given as batch 32 (stage 1) / 8 (stage 2), LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, LR 1e-5. The paper argues roughly 70% of the passages most similar to a query in open-domain QA sets should really be labeled positive.
papers.why_relevant: The strongest quantitative evidence in this survey that how you FILTER negatives matters more than how many you use: a ~4.5 nDCG@10 point swing from a threshold rule alone. It also gives concrete LoRA hyperparameters (r=16, alpha=32, lr=1e-5) that a top-of-leaderboard retriever actually used, and it warns that BM25-mined negatives were the worst teacher, which matters for Turkish where BM25 over unstemmed agglutinated surface forms is especially weak.

papers.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning
papers.approach: Train a single embedding so that its leading prefixes are themselves valid embeddings, by summing the task loss over a set of nested truncation dimensions (O(log d) granularities). No extra forward passes, no inference-time cost.
papers.key_results: Snippets cite up to 14x smaller embeddings at equal ImageNet-1K accuracy and up to 14x retrieval speedups. Vision numbers; I saw no text-retrieval numbers.
papers.why_relevant: Directly useful for the morphological channel encoder: you likely want that channel cheap and low-dimensional next to a full-size semantic vector. MRL lets you train one morph encoder and truncate to e.g. 128-256 dims for the concatenated dual-encoder score without retraining. Note the interaction with hard negatives is, as far as I found, unstudied.

papers.title: GISTEmbed: Guided In-sample Selection of Training Negatives for Text Embedding Fine-tuning
papers.approach: A separate, stronger 'guide' model scores every in-batch candidate at training time; batch items the guide judges too similar to the query-positive pair are dynamically masked out of the InfoNCE denominator rather than treated as negatives. Replaces the equal-utility assumption of in-batch negatives.
papers.key_results: Abstract claims consistent MTEB improvements across model sizes with the largest relative gains for smaller models, and SOTA in select categories. No specific numbers were given on the abstract page I fetched.
papers.why_relevant: The cleanest available mechanism for the in-batch false-negative problem you will hit hard: in a Turkish morphological dataset many batch items will be inflections of the same lemma, so random in-batch negatives are frequently near-positives. Implemented as GISTEmbedLoss / CachedGISTEmbedLoss in sentence-transformers, so it is a drop-in swap for MultipleNegativesRankingLoss. Caveat: the guide must itself be morph-aware, or it will mask out exactly your morph counterfactuals.

papers.title: Scaling Deep Contrastive Learning Batch Size under Memory Limited Setup (GradCache)
papers.approach: Decouples the contrastive-loss backward pass from the encoder backward pass by caching representation gradients, removing the batch-dimension data dependency. Gradients are then computed sub-batch by sub-batch at near-constant memory.
papers.key_results: Snippets report comparable retrieval accuracy to full-batch training with about a 20% runtime increase, and 8xV100 training reduced to a single GPU. Not verified from the PDF.
papers.why_relevant: The enabling trick for the whole recipe on a single A100/L4 Colab, which is your stated hardware. Because in-batch negatives are the free negatives, effective batch size is a first-class quality knob; GradCache (exposed as CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss / CachedGISTEmbedLoss in sentence-transformers) is how you get 1k-16k effective batch without the hardware. Budget ~20% extra wall-clock.

papers.title: AnglE-optimized Text Embeddings (AoE)
papers.approach: Argues the cosine objective has saturation zones where gradients vanish. Splits the embedding into real and imaginary parts and optimizes an angle difference in complex space, used alongside a cosine and an in-batch objective.
papers.key_results: Claims significant gains over cosine-only models on STS and MTEB. No numbers verified.
papers.why_relevant: Relevant only if part of your morph supervision is GRADED rather than binary, e.g. 'partial_trap is less wrong than morph_counterfactual'. CoSENTLoss and AnglELoss are the sentence-transformers losses that consume (text_a, text_b, float score) triples, which is the natural format if you assign each negative type a target similarity. If your labels stay binary, stick to InfoNCE/MNRL.

papers.title: Understanding the Behaviour of Contrastive Loss
papers.approach: Analyses InfoNCE as hardness-aware: the temperature tau controls how sharply the penalty concentrates on the hardest negatives. Formalises a uniformity-tolerance dilemma: low tau produces uniform, well-separated features but is intolerant of semantically similar samples; high tau spreads the penalty evenly over all negatives.
papers.key_results: Qualitative/analytical result plus vision experiments. I read search-result summaries only, not the paper.
papers.why_relevant: The theoretical justification for treating temperature as the key morphology knob. Your setting is the pathological case of the dilemma: morph counterfactuals are SUPPOSED to be pushed apart despite being semantically near-identical, so a low tau is what you want for the morph channel, but the same low tau on the semantic channel will punish legitimate paraphrases. Strong argument for per-channel temperatures, and for reporting tau in your ablations.

papers.title: Conan-embedding: General Text Embedding with More and Better Negative Samples
papers.approach: Two contributions: dynamic hard-negative mining, which re-mines negatives during training as the model improves rather than fixing them as a preprocessing step; and a cross-GPU balancing loss that shares negatives across devices and balances batch size across heterogeneous tasks.
papers.key_results: Reported as strong on the Chinese MTEB at publication. No numbers verified.
papers.why_relevant: Your typed negatives are static by construction, which means their difficulty decays as the model learns: after a few hundred steps the model may separate every morph_counterfactual trivially and the gradient dies. Periodic re-mining against the current checkpoint (and/or having the LLM synthesizer generate a fresh, harder batch) is the published fix. The cross-GPU/cross-batch negative sharing is the multi-GPU alternative to GradCache.

papers.title: Improving Text Embeddings with Large Language Models (e5-mistral-7b-instruct)
papers.authors_short: Wang, Yang, Huang, Yang, Majumder, Wei
papers.approach: Uses a proprietary LLM to generate synthetic (task description, query, positive, hard negative) tuples covering hundreds of thousands of embedding tasks in ~100 languages, then LoRA fine-tunes a decoder-only LLM with standard contrastive loss. No weakly-supervised pre-training stage at all.
papers.key_results: Search snippets report LoRA rank 16 and fewer than 1k training steps total, with strong MTEB results using no labeled data. Numbers not verified from the PDF.
papers.why_relevant: The closest published precedent for exactly what you are about to do: synthesize a training set with an LLM (including the hard negatives), then LoRA fine-tune. It is also the evidence that under 1k steps at rank 16 is enough, which is the single most effective guard against catastrophic forgetting, since a short low-rank run simply cannot move the base model far.

papers.title: TR-MTEB: A Comprehensive Benchmark and Embedding Model Suite for Turkish Sentence Representations
papers.approach: Builds a 26-dataset, six-task Turkish benchmark (classification, clustering, pair classification, retrieval, bitext mining, STS) and trains two Turkish-specific embedding models on a corpus of 34.2M weakly supervised Turkish sentence pairs using contrastive pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning.
papers.key_results: The 34.2M pair count and the two-stage contrastive pretraining + SFT description are from the fetched abstract page. The paper reports competitive performance and large gains over monolingual baselines; I did not obtain the per-task tables (the PDF fetch returned unreadable binary).
papers.why_relevant: The Turkish instantiation of the E5 two-stage recipe, and the obvious source for both your general-retrieval regression suite and a comparable weak-supervision corpus scale (34.2M pairs). Its retrieval subset is the natural 'did I forget general Turkish retrieval?' control to run before and after your morph LoRA.

papers.title: TurkColBERT: A Benchmark of Dense and Late-Interaction Models for Turkish Information Retrieval
papers.authors_short: Ezerceli, El Hussieni, Tas, Bayraktar, Terzioglu, Celebi, Asker
papers.approach: Two-stage adaptation pipeline: fine-tune English/multilingual encoders on Turkish NLI/STS first (semantic pre-adaptation), then convert them into ColBERT-style late-interaction retrievers trained on MS MARCO-TR via PyLate. Ten models benchmarked, including ColmmBERT-base-TR, colbert-hash-nano-tr (1.0M params), and turkish-e5-large (600M).
papers.key_results: From the fetched abstract: +13.8% mAP for ColmmBERT-base-TR on domain-specific tasks; colbert-hash-nano-tr retains over 71% of the large baseline's average mAP at 1.0M params; MUVERA indexing gives 0.54 ms query times. PEFT/LoRA and distillation are not mentioned in the abstract. Turkish is called morphologically rich but no morphological analysis appears in the abstract.
papers.why_relevant: Two things for your project. First, the NLI/STS-then-retrieval curriculum is an empirically used Turkish-specific ordering worth copying for the semantic encoder. Second, late interaction is the strongest alternative framing to a separate morph channel: token-level MaxSim naturally preserves suffix-level signal that a single pooled vector destroys, so it is a baseline your dual-encoder should be compared against rather than ignore.

papers.title: Negative Sampling Techniques in Information Retrieval: A Survey
papers.approach: Organizes negative sampling into six families: in-batch, cross-batch, BM25/ANCE-mined, denoised / false-negative-filtered, curriculum and dynamic hardness, and LLM-generated negatives.
papers.key_results: The six-family taxonomy is from my fetch of the PDF. The survey does not commit to universal numeric thresholds; it frames negative count, temperature, and false-negative rate as dataset-dependent calibration tasks. Treat any specific number attributed to it as unverified: I only obtained a summary-level read.
papers.why_relevant: Useful as the organizing skeleton for your related-work section, and it explicitly names 'LLM-generated negatives' as its own family, which is the category your synthesized typed-negative set falls into. Note this is a 2026 preprint past my training cutoff; I verified it exists by fetching it, but I have not seen it peer-reviewed.

techniques.name: Two-stage recipe: cheap in-batch-negative pre-training, then small hard-negative SFT
techniques.description: Stage 1 trains on a very large, noisy pair corpus with InfoNCE and in-batch negatives only, at the largest batch you can afford (mE5 used batch 32,768 for 30k steps per search snippets). Stage 2 is short, small-batch, and uses explicitly curated hard negatives, often plus distillation from a cross-encoder. E5, mE5, GTE, Qwen3-Embedding, NV-Embed and TR-MTEB all follow this shape.
techniques.evidence: E5 (2212.03533), mE5 (2402.05672), GTE (2308.03281), Qwen3-Embedding (fetched: ~150M weak pairs then ~7M labeled + ~12M filtered synthetic), TR-MTEB (fetched abstract: 34.2M weakly supervised Turkish pairs then SFT).
techniques.applicability: Map stage 2 onto your morphological set: it is small, expensive, and typed, which is exactly the stage-2 profile. Do not try to teach morphology in stage 1. If you skip stage 1 entirely (starting from an already-trained Turkish/multilingual encoder), you are effectively doing e5-mistral's synthetic-only recipe, which that paper shows works in under 1k steps.

techniques.name: Positive-aware hard-negative filtering (TopK-PercPos / TopK-MarginPos)
techniques.description: When mining negatives, do not take the top-K most similar passages. Discard any candidate whose similarity to the query exceeds a threshold anchored on the POSITIVE's score: 95% of the positive score (TopK-PercPos), or the positive score minus 0.05 (TopK-MarginPos), or an absolute 0.7 (TopK-Abs).
techniques.evidence: NV-Retriever (fetched fulltext): naive Top-K 0.5407 vs TopK-PercPos(95%) 0.5856 avg nDCG@10 on NQ/HotpotQA/FiQA with e5-large-unsupervised; the paper argues ~70% of the top-similar passages in open-domain QA should have been labeled positive.
techniques.applicability: Use this for any negatives you MINE from a Turkish corpus. Critically, do NOT apply it to your curated typed negatives: a morph_counterfactual is lexically near-identical to the gold and will score above 95% of the positive, so this filter would delete your entire signal. Run two negative pipelines with different rules (mined = filtered, curated = exempt) and keep that flag in your data schema.

techniques.name: Explicit false-negative masking inside the loss (Qwen3 rule)
techniques.description: Rather than filtering at mining time, mask candidates out of the InfoNCE denominator at loss time. Qwen3-Embedding sets mask m_ij = 0 when s_ij > s(q_i, d_i+) + 0.1, or when the candidate is the positive document itself; otherwise m_ij = 1. Their denominator also spans in-batch query-query, doc-doc, and cross-pair query-doc similarities, not just query-doc.
techniques.evidence: Qwen3-Embedding technical report, read from fetched HTML (arXiv 2506.05176v2).
techniques.applicability: The safest port is: apply the mask only to in-batch and mined negatives, and hard-exempt rows tagged as curated typed negatives. Log how often the mask fires on your morph negatives; if it fires on more than a few percent of them, your threshold is eating the dataset. That firing rate is itself a metric worth putting in the paper.

techniques.name: Guide-model in-batch negative masking (GISTEmbed)
techniques.description: A stronger auxiliary model scores every in-batch pairing during training and dynamically excludes items it judges related to the current query-positive pair, instead of assuming all in-batch items are valid negatives.
techniques.evidence: GISTEmbed (2402.16829, abstract fetched); available as GISTEmbedLoss and CachedGISTEmbedLoss in sentence-transformers per the fetched sbert loss-overview docs.
techniques.applicability: High value here because a Turkish morphological batch is full of accidental near-duplicates (same lemma, different suffixes). One-line swap from MultipleNegativesRankingLoss. Warning: choose the guide model carefully, since a guide that is morphologically blind will mask the very pairs you want contrasted. Consider a lexical/character-level guide, or disabling the guide for curated rows.

techniques.name: GradCache / cached MNRL for large effective batch on one GPU
techniques.description: Cache representation gradients so the contrastive loss backward pass is decoupled from the encoder backward pass, letting you compute encoder gradients sub-batch by sub-batch at near-constant memory. Roughly 20% runtime overhead for equivalent accuracy.
techniques.evidence: Gao et al., RepL4NLP 2021 (2101.06983), per search snippets; exposed as CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss / CachedGISTEmbedLoss per the fetched sbert docs.
techniques.applicability: This is what makes a serious recipe feasible on a single Colab A100/L4. Since in-batch negatives are free negatives and their count is a direct quality lever, treat mini_batch_size (memory) and batch_size (number of negatives) as separate knobs and tune them independently.

techniques.name: Per-channel temperature tuning
techniques.description: Temperature tau in InfoNCE controls how sharply the penalty concentrates on the hardest negatives, trading uniformity (separable features) against tolerance (not punishing genuinely similar items). Low tau = hard-negative-focused and intolerant; high tau = penalties spread evenly.
techniques.evidence: Wang & Liu, CVPR 2021 (2012.09740), search-snippet level. Note: neither the Qwen3 section I fetched nor the mE5 snippets stated an actual tau value; this is systematically underreported.
techniques.applicability: Your two encoders want opposite settings, which is a real finding you can claim. The morph channel must aggressively separate surface-similar-but-morphologically-different pairs (low tau); the semantic channel must tolerate paraphrase (higher tau). Run a small per-channel sweep (e.g. 0.01 / 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.1) and report it: it is cheap and almost nobody publishes it.

techniques.name: Dynamic / re-mined hard negatives instead of fixed preprocessing
techniques.description: Re-mine negatives against the current checkpoint during training so difficulty tracks model capability, rather than fixing the negative set once as a preprocessing step. Related: multi-granularity negative synthesis producing negatives at varying similarity levels for a coarse-to-fine curriculum.
techniques.evidence: Conan-embedding (2408.15710, snippet level); curriculum negative-sampling literature including CuSINeS (2404.00590) and multi-granularity hard-negative synthesis (2509.00842), both snippet level; named as its own family in the negative-sampling survey (2603.18005, fetched).
techniques.applicability: Directly addresses a failure mode you will hit: a fixed set of typed negatives becomes trivially separable within a few hundred steps and stops producing gradient. Since you are already planning LLM synthesis, you can regenerate a harder batch mid-training conditioned on which negative types the current model already handles, which would be a genuinely novel contribution in the morphological setting.

techniques.name: Curriculum over negative difficulty
techniques.description: Order training so easy/random negatives dominate early and hard negatives are phased in, sometimes with a different loss per stage and each stage initialized from the previous stage's best checkpoint.
techniques.evidence: Curriculum family named in the negative-sampling survey (2603.18005, fetched); CuSINeS and progressive-curriculum e-commerce work seen at snippet level only. I did NOT find a controlled ablation isolating curriculum gains for text embedders.
techniques.applicability: Natural ordering for you: random in-batch -> BM25/dense-mined topical negatives -> same_feature_wrong_content -> partial_trap -> morph_counterfactual. Your existing typed-negative taxonomy is already a difficulty ladder, which makes this cheap to implement and easy to ablate. Caveat: the evidence base is weaker than for negative filtering, so treat it as a hypothesis to test, not a settled recipe.

techniques.name: LoRA for embedders: rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-5, under 1k steps
techniques.description: Freeze the base encoder and train low-rank adapters on the attention/linear layers with the standard contrastive loss. Two independent top-tier retrievers converged on rank 16.
techniques.evidence: NV-Retriever (fetched): LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-5, batch 32 (stage 1) / 8 (stage 2). e5-mistral (2401.00368, snippet): LoRA rank 16, fewer than 1k training steps.
techniques.applicability: Concrete defaults to start from rather than guessing. The short-run plus low-rank combination is simultaneously your compute plan and your main anti-forgetting mechanism. For the dual-encoder, consider a separate adapter per channel over a shared frozen trunk: cheaper than two full encoders, and it makes the 'semantic only vs semantic+morph' ablation a matter of loading one adapter or two.

techniques.name: Matryoshka loss for a truncatable morphological channel
techniques.description: Sum the contrastive loss over nested prefix dimensions so the leading k dims of the embedding are independently valid. No extra forward passes, no inference cost. Available as MatryoshkaLoss, a loss MODIFIER that wraps any base loss (per the fetched sbert docs).
techniques.evidence: Kusupati et al., NeurIPS 2022 (2205.13147), snippet level; Qwen3-Embedding supports custom dims 1024/2560/4096 (fetched); sbert docs confirm MatryoshkaLoss composes with any base loss.
techniques.applicability: Lets you ship a small morph vector (128-256 dims) to concatenate onto a full semantic vector without training a separate small model, and lets you tune the semantic:morph dimension ratio post-hoc at eval time instead of retraining. I found no study of how MRL interacts with hard negatives, so validate rather than assume.

techniques.name: Graded-similarity losses (CoSENT / AnglE) for typed negatives
techniques.description: CoSENTLoss and AnglELoss consume (text_a, text_b, float_score) rather than triplets, and are described in the sbert docs as drop-in replacements with superior performance for that data format. AnglE additionally optimizes an angle in complex space to escape cosine saturation zones where gradients vanish.
techniques.evidence: AnglE / AoE (2309.12871, ACL 2024, snippet level); sbert loss-overview (fetched) for the data-format mapping.
techniques.applicability: Only worth it if you assign graded targets to your negative types (e.g. state_variant = 0.6, partial_trap = 0.4, morph_counterfactual = 0.1). Your typed taxonomy makes that modeling choice cheap. If you keep binary labels, stay on MNRL/GISTEmbed: the graded losses buy nothing.

techniques.name: Disable in-batch negatives when mixing heterogeneous task types
techniques.description: NV-Embed's stage 2 explicitly turns off the in-batch-negative trick once retrieval and non-retrieval data are blended, because in-batch pairings across task types are not meaningful negatives.
techniques.evidence: NV-Embed (2405.17428), search-snippet level.
techniques.applicability: Applies the moment you mix morphological triplets with general Turkish retrieval pairs in one training mixture. Either segregate by batch (each batch homogeneous in task type) or disable in-batch negatives for mixed batches. Getting this wrong is a silent bug of exactly the kind your repo notes already warn about for prompt prefixes.

techniques.name: Mining-model quality dominates mining-method cleverness
techniques.description: Which model you mine negatives with matters more than ensembling several. NV-Retriever's ablation put e5-mistral-7b-instruct at 0.5810 avg nDCG@10 versus BM25 at 0.5002; a 4-model ensemble gave only 0.5825.
techniques.evidence: NV-Retriever (fetched fulltext).
techniques.applicability: Sharper for Turkish than for English: BM25 over unstemmed agglutinated surface forms is a weak miner, and worse, BM25-mined negatives for a morphology task will be biased toward shared-root-different-suffix items, which are either exactly what you want or exactly a false negative depending on the query. Mine with your best available Turkish/multilingual dense model, and use BM25 only as a deliberate source of morphologically confusable candidates that you then hand to the LLM to label.

techniques.name: Model merging (slerp) over SFT checkpoints
techniques.description: After supervised fine-tuning, spherically interpolate several checkpoints saved during that run into a single model, rather than picking one.
techniques.evidence: Qwen3-Embedding (fetched HTML): slerp applied to multiple checkpoints saved during fine-tuning, described as a distinct third training stage.
techniques.applicability: A near-free robustness win and a plausible partial mitigation for over-specialization, since averaging weights pulls back toward the pre-fine-tuning region. Cheap to try because you will be saving checkpoints anyway. For LoRA specifically this means averaging adapter weights.

techniques.name: Anti-forgetting protocol and how to measure it
techniques.description: Keep the fine-tuning run short (one epoch), the LR low, and gradient norm moderate; prefer adapters over full fine-tuning; optionally merge checkpoints. Measure forgetting by re-running a held-out general benchmark before and after.
techniques.evidence: e5-mistral's under-1k steps at rank 16 (snippet). LoRA-forgets-less-than-full-FT is well supported in the LLM literature (e.g. scaling laws for forgetting, 2401.05605, snippet level). The one concrete embedding number I saw was a general MTEB drop from 0.6463 to 0.6320 after domain-specific training, but that came from a semantic-caching applied paper (2504.02268) via a search snippet, not a dedicated forgetting study, so treat it as illustrative only.
techniques.applicability: Concretely: freeze a pre-LoRA baseline on the four trmteb BEIR-format sets you already run (scifact-tr, nfcorpus-tr, arguana-tr, fiqa-tr) and report delta nDCG@10 alongside your morph-eval gain. A morph gain reported without the general-retrieval delta is not publishable, and your existing results_local cache from eval_semantic_encoders.py already gives you that baseline nearly for free.

techniques.name: Instruction/prompt-prefix consistency between training and eval
techniques.description: Instruction-tuned embedders encode a fixed template; Qwen3 uses "{Instruction} {Query}<|endoftext|>" for queries and no instruction for documents. E5-family models use query: / passage:.
techniques.evidence: Qwen3-Embedding instruction format read from fetched HTML; E5 prefix convention from the E5 papers at snippet level.
techniques.applicability: Your CLAUDE.md already flags this as the classic silent bug for zero-shot comparison. It gets worse after fine-tuning: whatever prefix you train the LoRA with becomes load-bearing, so an eval script still using the base model's original prefix will silently sandbag your own fine-tuned model. Pin the prefix in the adapter config and assert it at eval time.

gaps: I found no paper that does contrastive fine-tuning of a retriever using explicitly MORPHOLOGICAL typed hard negatives, in Turkish or any other agglutinative language. The morphology-aware Turkish work I surfaced is about tokenization/segmentation (Morpheus, HeceTokenizer, subword-strategy studies), not about negative construction for contrastive retrieval. This looks like a genuine gap your project sits in. Caveat: several of those Turkish tokenization preprints are dated 2026 and past my training cutoff, so I saw them only as search-result titles and could not vet them.

Direct conflict between two techniques, unresolved in the literature: every published false-negative filter (NV-Retriever's TopK-PercPos at 95% of the positive score, Qwen3's s_ij > s_pos + 0.1 mask, GISTEmbed's guide-model masking) is a SIMILARITY-THRESHOLD rule, and a morphological counterfactual is by construction extremely similar to the gold passage. Applied naively, all three would discard exactly the negatives your dataset exists to provide. No paper I found addresses filtering when high surface similarity is the point rather than a false-negative signal. This needs to be an explicit design decision and probably an ablation.

Temperature values are systematically unreported. The Qwen3 section I fetched gives the loss formula with tau but never states its value; the mE5 snippets say hyperparameters follow English E5 without giving a number. I could not extract a single concrete production temperature from any primary source I read.

No guidance exists on how many typed negatives per query is right for a morphology task. The only hard numbers I have are from generic retrieval: NV-Retriever used 4 per query in ablations, 1 in stage 1 and 5 in stage 2 for the released model; one snippet mentioned a 10-negatives-per-query setup. Your eval set has ~10 candidates per query, so whether all types go into one InfoNCE denominator or are sampled per step is an open choice.

Catastrophic forgetting in EMBEDDING fine-tuning is poorly studied compared to LLM fine-tuning. Nearly all the forgetting literature I found (O-LoRA, CLoRA, EWCLoRA, OPLoRA, scaling laws for forgetting) is about generative LLMs. The single embedding-specific number I saw (general MTEB 0.6463 -> 0.6320 after domain training) came from a search snippet on an applied semantic-caching paper, not a controlled study, and I would not cite it as evidence.

Matryoshka representation learning has, as far as I found, never been studied in combination with hard-negative training or with a two-channel / dual-encoder score fusion. Its published wins are vision classification and retrieval speedups. Treat MRL-for-the-morph-channel as an untested engineering idea, not a supported one.

The curriculum-over-negative-difficulty idea is named as a category in the negative-sampling survey and appears in applied papers (CuSINeS, progressive e-commerce mining, multi-granularity synthesis), but I did not find a clean controlled ablation isolating curriculum gains for general-purpose text embedders. Evidence here is materially weaker than for the filtering techniques.

I could not read the TR-MTEB PDF (the fetch returned unreadable binary), so I have the abstract-level recipe (34.2M weakly supervised Turkish pairs, contrastive pretraining plus SFT) but no loss details, no temperature, no batch size, and none of its per-task retrieval tables. Worth a manual read since it is the single most directly comparable Turkish system.

Several sources I relied on are dated 2025-2026 and sit at or past my knowledge cutoff: the negative-sampling survey (arXiv 2603.18005), TurkColBERT (2511.16528), TR-MTEB (Findings EMNLP 2025), Qwen3-Embedding (2506.05176). I verified these exist by fetching them, but I cannot vouch for their reception, peer-review status, or whether their claims have held up.

Nothing I found addresses how to weight or fuse a semantic channel and a morphological channel at scoring time (concatenation, learned gate, score interpolation). BGE-M3's self-knowledge distillation across dense/sparse/multi-vector heads is the nearest analogue, but it fuses retrieval FUNCTIONALITIES, not linguistic channels.
confidence:
Medium-high overall, with sharply uneven verification per item. Please read the per-paper 'verified' field rather than treating this uniformly.

Strongest ground (fetched full text, numbers copied directly off the page): NV-Retriever's mining taxonomy, thresholds (TopK-PercPos 95%, TopK-MarginPos 0.05, TopK-Abs 0.7, N=10), the nDCG@10 ablation table (0.5407 naive vs 0.5856 PercPos, with per-dataset NQ/HotpotQA/FiQA splits), mining-model comparison (e5-mistral 0.5810 vs BM25 0.5002), and training config (LoRA r=16, alpha=32, lr=1e-5, batch 32/8). Also solid: Qwen3-Embedding's false-negative mask rule (s_ij > s_pos + 0.1), data sizes (~150M / ~7M / ~12M), the 0.7 cosine filter, per-size dims (1024/2560/4096), and instruction format, all read from the fetched HTML. The sentence-transformers loss-to-data-format mapping is from the official fetched docs.

Weaker ground (abstract only): GISTEmbed's mechanism is confirmed but I have no numbers for it. TR-MTEB's 34.2M-pair figure and two-stage description come from the fetched landing page, not the PDF (which failed to parse). TurkColBERT's +13.8% mAP, 71%-retention and 0.54ms figures are abstract claims I did not verify in tables. The negative-sampling survey gave me a taxonomy but no reliable numbers.

Weakest ground (search snippets only, treat every number as unconfirmed): SimCSE's 76.3/81.6 STS figures, mE5's batch 32,768 / 30k steps, MRL's 14x claims, GradCache's ~20% overhead, e5-mistral's rank-16 / under-1k-steps, and all NV-Embed architecture details (512 latents, 8 heads). These are widely repeated numbers I believe are correct, but I read them in search summaries, not on the source pages.

Two things I want to flag as MY INFERENCE rather than reported fact: (1) the claim that similarity-threshold false-negative filters will destroy morphological counterfactuals is my reasoning from the mechanism, not something any paper states. It is the most important point in this survey and also the least sourced. (2) The per-channel-temperature recommendation follows from the uniformity-tolerance dilemma, but no paper I read applies it to a dual-channel setup. Both are hypotheses your project would be testing, which is arguably good news for novelty.

I did not verify author lists or exact venues beyond what the fetched pages stated, and I did not confirm publication status for the 2026-dated preprints. Ten distinct searches and seven fetches were run; no files were created or modified.
